subtopic: REVENUE TO BE SECURED AND BURDEN EQUALIZED BY INCOME RATHER THAN COMMODITY TAXATION
REVENUE TO BE SECURED AND BURDEN EQUALIZED BY INCOME RATHER THAN COMMODITY TAXATION
speechtext:
Whereas, it is becoming increasingly apparent that the present methods and extent of federal taxation are inadequate to meet our requirement, and
Whereas, an extension of the principle of commodity taxation has been suggested as a means of meeting the situation, and
Whereas, the drastic fall in price levels and the consequent increase in the purchasing value of money has seriously affected the producer and the business man, while being of corresponding benefit to those whose incomes, derived from certain classes of bonds, mortgages, etc., are still undiminished, if not increased.
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration, in order to equalize the weight of taxation and that an additional burden be not placed upon the shoulders of those who are already the chief sufferers from present conditions, that any increase in taxation found necessary should take the form of adjustments in the Income Tax Act, in order that those best able to pay should be the first and most heavily affected.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I am presenting this afternoon is worded in such a manner as to practically speak for itself. I think it will be agreed that owing to the drastic fall in commodity prices and the general depression which exists, the question of taxation assumes an added importance at the present time. May I say at the beginning that I fully appreciate the difficulties with which the government is confronted in times like this. I believe that the right hon. the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet are sparing neither time nor energy m endeavouring to meet the situation and to make conditions better in Canada. They are faced with a very difficult task and my hope is that the resolution which I am sponsoring this afternoon may assist in pointing the way to a better method of securing the moneys required from the people for the carrying on of the business of government in a manner that will 'be fair and equitable to all.
There is a very old saying that the only two things man is sure of in this life are death

Federal Taxation-Mr. Lucas
and taxation. I believe that the average man avoids meeting both as long as possible. The question of taxation is an old one. It was fought out by the British people many centuries ago when the principle was established that there should be no taxation without representation. Under our democratic form-of government the theory is that if the people are well and truly represented laws will be made and a system of taxation devised that will be fair and equitable to all. If this were really true, then if adversity did come, how appropriate would be those lines which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), when bringing down his budget last year, quoted from the chronicles of the Pilgrim Fathers:
It wonderfully encourageth men in their duties when they see the burthen equally borne.
If we are passing through a depression for which no individual is responsible, then all should bear their share according to their ability to carry the load. The income tax system in Canada was first introduced as a war measure and was known as the Income War Tax Act of 1917. In the fiscal year 1930-31 the amount derived from this source was $71,048,022. Of this amount of income tax collected, $26,624,181 was paid by 143,601 individuals, and S44,423,841 by 7,603 corporations. The receipts of last year's income tax have been exceeded only -once since its imposition, when in 1921-22 $78,600,000 was received. In that year individuals paid $39,820,000 and corporations $38,863,000. It is worthy of note that practically the same percentage of people contribute -to the income tax in Canada as do the taxpayers in the United States, namely, one and one-half per cent.
In the United States the income tax system was first introduced ahout the time of the Civil war and was later found to be unconstitutional; but so convinced were the people of that country that the system was
a fair and equitable means of raising revenue that they amended their constitution, a very difficult thing to do when we consider that they had to receive the consent of three-fifths of the state legislatures. This consent was received in 1913, and so successful has been tihe income tax in the United States that in the year 1925 nearly fifty-seven per cent of the total federal revenue came from income tax collections. In the same year in Great Britain over fifty per cent of the total revenue was derived from the income tax, and in Canada less then twenty per cent comes therefrom, so that the income tax in Canada, comparatively speaking, is not a burdensome tax. It might be further stated -that to-day Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Italy, Czechoslovakia, India, Japan, South Africa, Australia, the United States, Jamaica and other countries have adopted and retain the income tax -as a means of raising revenue.
We find that a number of the provinces have either adopted or are about to adopt the system of taxations on incomes. I believe I am right in stating that the province of Quebec at the last sitting of its legislature imposed a one per cent income tax upon corporations. Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house have frequently been accused of bringing forward and presenting for the consideration of the house resolutions and suggestions which have been said to be wholly academic in character, vague in their application, and hav-

Federal Taxation-Mr. Speakman
ing no immediate relation to the everyday problems of the present time. As to whether this accusation is wholly justified, that is another story, but one which I do not propose to discuss at the moment save to say this, that there is a remote possibility that some of these so-called academic resolutions which suggest more or less fundamental changes in our social and economic systems may in point of fact be just as practical and possibly of very much greater value to the future of this country than many of the so-called practical suggestions, the absence of which is so greatly deplored by our critics. However that may be, no such criticism can be offered in respect of the present resolution, dealing as it does with a matter which is of immediate import and of immediate effect upon the wellbeing of every individual citizen of this country, as well as upon the financial necessities of the state, and which from every point of view is at once highly opportune and eminently practical.
Nor is this proposal advanced, Mr. Speaker, with any purpose of embarrassing the administration. On the contrary, it should be welcomed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and by his associates in that it affords an opportunity to the members of this house of pronouncing upon this important question, and if supported by the majority of the members here the resolution will greatly strengthen the hands of the government in dealing with a matter which in the very nature of things is bound to be highly unpopular in many influential quarters.
The hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) in introducing this resolution has presented the case with such clarity and has supported his contention with such a wealth of irrefutable logic that little remains to be said by myself in seconding the resolution or by others who may speak in its support save to reiterate, to amplify and stress the arguments which have already been advanced in my hon. friend's most excellent and convincing address, and to anticipate so far as possible some of the objections which may be raised by those who are opposed to this method of taxation.
As to the necessity of increased taxation at the present time, little need be said. We are all familiar with the position of the national exchequer to-day, and if further argument were required it may be found by a glance at the estimates which are now before the house, estimates in which in a noble effort to balance the budget we find that most of the services have been cut most drastically, that staffs in many of the departments have been materially reduced, and that throughout the service the
salaries have been slashed to a point which in some cases will fail to come up to the level of a satisfactory or even a decent livelihood. We find that there is a net reduction in the proposed expenditure appearing in the estimates for the coming year of some 843,000,000. Indeed, the actual reduction is more than that figure would indicate, because we also find that there is an increase of some $13,000,000 of interest on the public debt to be paid during the coming year. So the net reduction in controllable expenditure will be in the neighbourhood of $56,000,000. I am not at the moment going to discuss the wisdom or otherwise of this policy. I am not at the moment going to analyze the situation and consider whether the ultimate effect of these drastic cuts will be to relieve or to intensify the difficulties of the situation, but for the moment looking at it wholly from the point of view of the administration and the Prime Minister, the necessity of balancing the budget at all costs, we must realize that even these sacrifices in themselves will not achieve the objective and bring about a balanced budget without some increase in our national revenues, which means increased taxation. This fact I think is generally recognized throughout the country, and the question being asked at the present time on all sides and in many quarters with anxiety and deep concern is as to what method of taxation may be adopted and upon whose shoulders will the added burden fall. Indications have already appeared in the press suggesting the methods which may be adopted, suggesting increases in our present fields of taxation as well as new fields which may be explored. Those indications have been taken so seriously in many quarters as to form the basis of many comments, adverse and otherwise, and to have aroused much discussion both public and private, as well as inspiring many resolutions by various organized bodies of business men. Of these resolutions it would be premature for me to speak at this moment, until we know more definitely the intentions of the government. May I, however, make this comment? All of the resolutions which I have seen and all of the discussion which I have heard are based upon the anticipation that these increases will take the form of increased commodity taxation of one sort or another, either by way of an increased sales tax, a turnover tax or what not; but whatever method is adopted, it seems to be universally expected that the increase will follow that principle of commodity taxation. I most fervently hope, Mr. Speaker, that such will not be the case.

Federal Taxation-Mr. Speakman
It is not my intention at the moment to enter upon any general discussion either of conditions or of taxation, but may I comment upon one phase of both which is a factor, and a most potent factor, to be considered at the present time and in the present situation. I think it is generally recognized that in this country is sufficient wealth to enable us to meet all our obligations, to meet every demand made upon us, and to provide an acceptable livelihood for all our people. It is also, I think, generally recognized that this wealth is not equitably distributed amongst all classes of our population. That some greater equality of distribution should be brought about is a consummation devoutly to be desired. The method by which it may be accomplished is a problem which is as yet unsolved and towards the solution of which, so far as I know, no full and comprehensive plan has yet been offered. It has been stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that all of us are anxious that this should be done. It has also been stated, and by the same hon. gentleman, that so far no plan has been offered and that this desirable consummation remains but a pious aspiration. I am not challenging that statement, nor am I attempting to suggest to this house any such full or comprehensive plan.
But in admitting that this problem does exist, in admitting that this inequality of wealth is present in our land, we are also admitting a certain definite responsibility, in that so far as we have power within our hands to control the situation we should use that power to rectify rather than enhance it. At the moment and without discussing more deep-seated, more fundamental changes of any kind, the most potent weapon we have in our hands for this purpose is the power of taxation, and in the resolution we are proposing that this weapon should be used, and should be used effectively. As stated in the [DOT]esolution itself, while the great body of producers in Canada have suffered, and are suffering, tremendous losses through the tragically low prices of all our primary products, a small but disproportionately wealthy class of our citizens-who were in a position to invest in the recent issues of national and provincial bonds, for example-are actually profiting from the situation. Amidst the crash of falling values there is one commodity which has not only retained but actually increased in its market value-the commodity of money. Those who own and control that commodity are undoubtedly enriched both by the higher interest rates which are now prevailing-higher than I have ever known in 
respect of dominion or provincial bonds during my residence in this country-and by the increased purchasing power of each dollar. This being the case,-and I think no one here will challenge the accuracy of the statement-equity and sound policy alike would indicate that any increased taxation should be levied, not upon the goods already produced below cost, but upon the money itself-upon the one commodity which shows a constantly increasing profit.
Revenue from taxation, whether direct or indirect, must in the end be paid out of income, and the soundest and most economical way to collect that tax upon income is to collect it directly. Unquestionably, Mr. Speaker, the inevitable effect of present price levels, with the value of money and commodities so completely out of line-the money value of commodities so extremely low, and the commodity value of money so excessively high-must be to make the rich richer, and the poor poorer. The main corrective that we have for this situation is, as I stated, our control over taxation, the power and authority which lies in this house to take for the use of the national exchequer a fair proportion of all incomes, particularly of the larger ones. The argument which is most frequently advanced by those who are opposed to any increase of taxation upon the larger incomes is that it is to these incomes you must look for investment, for the expansion of existing industry and for the creation and establishment of new industry. While this is partially true, it is also true that it is to the multitude of those earning small incomes we must look rather than to the comparatively few wealthy individuals when we seek a- market for the products of our farms and our factories. Unquestionably a million dollars divided among ten thousand individuals is of infinitely greater value to the agricultural, industrial and commercial life of this countiy than the same sum in the hands of a dozen wealthy men, because the smaller the income-and this is a truism, but it is so frequently forgotten apparently that it is well to reiterate it at times-the greater proportion of that income that must be spent upon the so-called necessities of life; in other words, upon the goods which are produced in this and in other countries. As a result, the greater the number amongst whom purchasing power is distributed the greater must be demand for those goods. For after all, as a consumer, the consuming capacity of the wealthiest man is extremely limited, and he can only spend a comparatively trivial percentage of his wealth on those goods which

Federal Taxation-Mr. Speakman
are produced. Any reduction therefore in these smaller incomes must lead to a general curtailment of consumption throughout the country, it must lower the standard of living for thousands of our families, and it must mean a corresponding diminution in the already inadequate markets which are available to our producers.
It is on these grounds, Mr. Speaker, that we are urging the adoption of this resolution, as well as upon the ground of immediate expediency. For after all there are still two main pillars upon which every sound system of taxation should rest, that each individual shall contribute to the state in proportion, first, to his ability to pay, and, second, to the benefits which he derives from living and doing business in the country. Both of these may be expressed in terms of income. May I venture, then, to suggest to the Minister of Finance that just as they say, gold is where you find it, so the place to look for money is where money is. At the present time it is not in the hands of the producer, the wage earner or the low-salaried man, but of those whose incomes are derived from the possession of money itself. These by means of certain adjustments of the Income Tax Act may be made to contribute a much larger proportion to our federal revenues than is at present the case.
It is true that in suggesting the most obvious and the most logical source for increasing our national revenue will be found amongst those who possess the largest part of the wealth of this country we are suggesting a very radical departure from prevailing practice. It is not too much to say that the opposite has been the definite policy of this and of most other countries. An extremely vivid illustration of this practice will be found in the juxtaposition of two incidents which took place in this house on Friday last. Two bills were then introduced, the first providing for something over 811,000,000 for the Canadian National Railways, necessitated in large part for the protection of the bondholders of the railway in respect of interest due. The second bill was that which provided for a ten per cent cut in 'the salaries of our civil servants. These two motions taken together, Mr. Speaker, were to me most significant. The interest upon capital is sacred, it must ibe protected; the wages and salaries of our working people must be sacrificed upon the altar of financial necessity and to provide a balanced budget. Yet why ghould this be? It is true, as has 'been stated more than once, that the interests of our
bondholders are protected by statute and by our given word. So, too, were the salaries of our civil servants. Were those two motions symbolic of the relative status we accord those two great partners in our national development, in all our national undertakings, capital and labour? I trust not, and if not, if it is our policy to accord to both an equality of status, of dignity and of respect, the income tax affords us our opportunity.
May I suggest also, Mr. Speaker, that we should have some consideration for our more wealthy citizens. We should not refuse to them the glorious opportunities which have been accorded our civil employees. As I heard the Prime Minister and listened to that splendid eloquence with which he illustrated and illumined the really noble sentiments which he uttered, as he spoke of the patriotic motives which actuated at least part of our civil service in accepting the reduction, not reluctantly or grudgingly but gladly and joyfully, taking a deep and keen pleasure in this opportunity of being of service to their country in her hour of need, I thought to myself: Why should we selfishly restrict this pleasure to a limited class? Why not afford that same opportunity and grant that same privilege to the relatively wealthy men and women who are in Canada to-day? In this, as in other matters, our motto should be equal rights to all and special privileges to none.
I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of all the foregoing facts, and in spite of the glowing words of the Prime Minister, this suggestion might prove unpopular in some quarters, and it has been stated, as indicated also by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) in his address, that the chief exponents of an increased income tax are those who, like the organized farmers, do not come under this form of taxation. That the average farmer does not pay income tax unfortunately is true, but that does not militate against tihe soundness of the proposal. If you consider for a moment, Mr. Speaker, the situation in which agriculture finds itself, with the price levels of all the commodities produced so low, you will readily appreciate the fact that it is the misfortune of the farmer and not his fault that he does not pay income tax. Nothing would please the average farmer more-not to be taxed; I am not going to say anyone likes to be taxed1-than to operate upon such a basis as would bring him within the terms of our Income Tax Act, and may I further add that the great percentage of our federal revenues always have been obtained through one form or another of

Indeed, it is this very fact that the average farmer does not and cannot pay any form of income tax, that bis income and profits alike have been reduced far below the vanishing point, which affords the most potent and cogent argument in favour of this resolution.

That being true, that the great incomes have come almost wholly from special privileges granted to these groups by this house, it does seem to me only fair, it is nothing but justice, that they should pay back in income tax, and quite a saucy

Federal Taxation-Mr. Rhodes
income tax too, out of the income that special privilege has allowed them to accumulate. Every other point I can think of has been covered and I cannot see how this house can vote against the resolution with times as they are at the moment.

One point
that might be given consideration, a point that has not been recognized, is the importance of drawing a distinction between income derived from investments and income from salaries. I believe that distinction is drawn in the income tax legislation in the old country. When discussing this question in the past, urging further taxation of incomes derived from bonds and dividends, we have always heard of the hypothetical case of the poor widow who would be severely penalized by a tax on an income of three or four thousand dollars derived from investments. Some of us did not give much consideration to an argument of that kind and I do not think it is worthy of consideration. In my opinion a distinction should be drawn between income derived from investments, which is a permanent thing, and income derived from salary.
Let us take the case of the widow, which has been referred to in the past, whose husband has left her a large investment. She has that income going on from year to year-
She may not be living to-day.

That is a remark one might expect from that quarter of the house. Her husband, as I was saying, might have left her an income derived from a large investment, and she is in an entirely different position from the widow whose wage-earner died and left her without any income.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: She pays no tax.

In both cases, while the
husbands were alive, the income might have been the same, derived in one case from an investment and in the other from a salary. I am not going to discuss the matter at any length; it has been very ably presented; but I do want to call the attention of the house to that point, that there should be a distinction between incomes derived from investments and those derived from salaries or made perhaps by conducting a certain business.

What about the sessional indemnity of members of the House of Commons? Does the hon. member refer to those as being exempt?

Just at the moment I do
not feel called upon to discuss that question. Now that it has been raised, however, I may observe that, as everyone knows, the sessional indemnity of $4,000 is not all income by any means. I think everyone knows that while we are taxed on $4,000 we are taxed on money that we have to spend in many ways.
I do not know why the hon. member should have raised the question at the moment.
You spoke of salaries.

Just at the moment I do
not care to discuss that question. speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not help contrasting the attitude of those who have spoken on this resolution to-day with the attitude of the house when the proposals were first made in the year 1917.
I recall the situation at that time very well indeed. In fact, the then Minister of Finance, the Right Hon. Sir Thomas White, in bringing down his proposals, was at pains to point out that the provinces and municipalities were limited in their scope of direct taxation whereas the dominion field was unlimited and very much larger in its area than that afforded to either the provinces or the municipalities. He took the point of view at that time that the question of income tax was one purely for the provinces and municipalities. He said on that occasion:
As I have stated, the provinces and the municipalities are confined to direct taxation, and I have not regarded it as expedient, except in case of manifest public necessity, such as I believe exists at the present time, that the dominion should invade the field to which the provinces are solely confined for the raising of their revenue.
My more particular purpose in making reference to that question is this. Those who have spoken on this resolution-I regret that more have not done so-have apparently overlooked entirely the fact that the income taxpayer is called upon to pay not only by the dominion but by the municipal and provincial treasuries as well; and there is a disposition in both those fields to increase very heavily the burden of the income taxpayer. As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me rightly, in

Federal Taxation-Mr. Rhodes

one province alone it is contemplated during the present year to double the existing income tax.
One would rather gather from the remarks of hon. gentlemen who support the resolution that there has been a marked disparity between the income taxpayer and others who pay taxes in the country, very much to the advantage of the income taxpayer. Particular reference was made to the man who pays very large income tax. Whatever may be said with respect to the rates themselves, so far as their application to individuals is concerned, there is nothing whatsoever in that contention. Take the case of our own country last year. We had a total of 143,601 persons who paid income tax, the total amount paid by them being a little more than $26,500,000; 1 speak now of purely personal income tax. Of that number, some 13,447 paid no less a sum than $23,256,550; in other words, the number which I have just indicated paid that sum as against $3,367,631 paid by some 130,154 income tax payers in the lower categories.
How much had they left after they paid that large income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will be
able to answer that question himself by an examination of the income tax tables, but the figures which I will give in a moment will afford an answer in part.
I regret I could not follow the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas). I heard him only indistinctly at this distance, whether it was because I am slightly deaf as a result of a cold or because of the acoustic properties of this chamber, I do not know. However, I heard him make one or two particular remarks, to which I will refer. If I have missed others, I hope he will understand why I am not referring to them as well.
The hon. gentleman referred to the income tax in Great Britain as compared to the tax in Canada. He must bear in mind that not only have we a dominion income tax, but we have in addition municipal and provincial income taxes. There is another very important point which should be kept in mind when making comparisons with the Canadian income tax, and that is that our tax must bear some reasonable relationship to the rates prevailing in the United States.
How many provinces in Canada have an income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that question off hand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Four, at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does not require any
perfect argument to indicate the danger of our income tax in Canada being substantially out of line with the rate of taxation in the republic to the south. Capital is very sensitive and it will not remain long upon one side of an imaginary line if it can transfer to the other and be more lightly burdened. However, this is altogether apart from the merits of the question of whether we have or have not at the present time a sufficiently high income tax in Canada, and upon this point I will touch later on.
At the present time low as our income tax may be as compared to the tax in Great Britain or as compared to the rates prevailing in 1921, as pointed out by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), they are substantially higher than the taxes applied in the United States. I have the figures before me, but I will not weary the house by reading them in full; I will quote only a few examples. A married man without dependents with an income of $4,000 would pay in Canada an income tax of $16 as compared with $5.63 in the United States. An income of $8,000 would pay in Canada $128 as compared to $56.25 in the United States. An income of $14,000 would pay $536 in Canada and $258.75 in the United States. An income of $20,000 would pay $1,232 in Canada and $618.75 in the United States. A $30,000 income pays $2,880 in Canada and $1,488.75 in the United States.
Are those the present United States figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; I am not speaking of the proposed increased taxation.
In making a comparison between the rates of income tax in Canada and in the United States I would point out to the right hon. metnbeT for Mackenzie that he must not overlook the fact that federal, state and municipal bonds are tax exempt in the United States. This makes a vast difference in dealing with the question of income taxes, as this condition does not obtain in Canada.
Those bonds command a higher rate on the market and for that reason there is a lower return to the purchaser.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see how that has any bearing upon the question of income tax.
It means that the bondholder receives a lower rate of interest on his -bond because it is tax free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That depends entirely upon what the income of the man may be. He

Federal Taxation-Mr. Rhodes
might very well be able to afford to purchase tax free bonds returning one per cent if it reduced his income tax below a figure which would involve a high degree of taxation.
A man receiving an income of $50,000 pays $6,704 in Canada and $4,563.75 in the United States. An income of $100,000 pays $19,064 in Canada and $15,743.75 in the United States. We come now to the class of which most of us only read in the story books but which seems to give considerable worry to my hon. friends diagonally opposite. A man with an income of half a million dollars pays an income tax of $162,952 in Canada and $115,743.75 in the United States. The man who may have a million dollars of income pays $362,928 in Canada whereas in the United States he would pay a tax of $240,743.75.
Not to go at length into the merits, it might be interesting to know that even with a rate which is regarded by hon. gentlemen diagonally opposite as being too low, during the last fiscal year the income taxpayers of Canada paid twenty-three per cent of our total federal income. It is worthy of note that since the income tax first came into vogue fourteen years ago, the income taxpayers have paid into the treasury no less a sum than $743,000,000.
The average would be a little more than twenty-three per cent, having regard to the higher rates which have prevailed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Having regard to the fact that the present rate is much lower as compared to the years preceding, the rate in former years would be substantially higher, although I have not the exact figures in that regard.
The hon. member for Camrose referred to some remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in the house last week, wherein he indicated that the cost of living had diminished to the extent of 14.4 per cent. My hon. friend said that that argument might be turned around and it might be said that money was now worth 14.4 per cent more in purchasing power. Very good. Then he said: Why should the income tax payer not pay an extra ten per cent, or in other words have his income cut to that extent in the same manner as civil servants were called upon to make a contribution of ten per cent? I would think perhaps in the circumstances the income tax payer would be very happy to accept that as a final settlement of the question. But the point I want to make in connection with that is that it is not at all in keeping with the resolution of my hon.
friend. His resolution, stripped of its verbiage and brought down to bare essentials, means this, that to the extent that we require additional taxation in this country we must take the whole of it from the income tax payer. That is rather a far-fetched proposition, it seems to me. Leaving aside altogether the question of the comparative rates as between ourselves and the United States, leaving aside the question of the merits as to just how high income taxation can be, one must realize there is a limit beyond which you may not go in any field of taxation. There is a line and if you attempt to go beyond it, it will serve to defeat the very object you have in mind. You are not going to produce revenue in proportion to the amount that you increase taxation. That has been found out not only in this country but in other countries times without number.
But having said so much, let me say this to my hon. friend: I would not take exception to a resolution which took the sense of the house as indicating that there should be a substantial increase in income taxation, although I might point out that it would not be incumbent upon me at this stage and upon a resolution of this kind, to pronounce any policy with respect to the attitude of the government in regard to the matter of increased taxation. But that is not what he has submitted. Apart altogether from any inequalities which are bound to arise in taxation, he would debar us from entering any other avenue of taxation which we might very properly enter, and he would have the whole burden with respect to any increase in revenue w'hieh we might require, laid upon the income tax payer.
He asks the government only to give consideration to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite so, but were the principle in this resolution to be accepted, the government would be debarred from entering any other field of taxation open to it. That is as I read the resolution. If I have misread it, I am open to correction. The hon. member's resolution reads:
Any increase in taxation found necessary should take the form of adjustments in the Income Tax Act, in order that those best able to pay should be the first and most heavily affected.
I do not think I am doing my hon. friend any injustice and I believe I am putting a proper interpretation on the resolution when I say that, bearing that in mind, we are ab^ solutely precluded from accepting it. Having

said so much, I would hope that it would suit the purposes of my hon. friend to withdraw his resolution, but if that does not meet with his wishes, especially having in mind the fact that there is a slimly attended house and the further fact that so few have spoken on the resolution, I would take the opportunity of moving the adjournment of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, before you put the
motion, may I interject that I think my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) is perhaps taking rather i drastic course with respect to this matter, f intended to say something about this contention that if the government accepted the motion, this would be the only field of taxation which the government would be allowed to enter. If my hon. friend will look at the concluding words of the resolution, he will see that such is hardly the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I moved the adjournment only for the purpose of enlarging the discussion because apparently nobody else wished to speak. If any other hon. member wishes to speak, with the consent of the house, I will withdraw my motion.

I should
like to occupy the time of the house for a moment or two on this question. I am sorry I do not get out of the resolution the same meaning that the Minister of Finance has taken. I do not believe that if it were accepted he would be precluded from increasing taxation in other fields. If he were, cf course I can quite see the handicap under which he would be acting in accepting the resolution.
As was very aptly pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) the attitude of the government with regard to taxation has been to increase taxes upon commodities. There have been substantial increases and last year the then Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), introduced a substantial change in the income tax which was not carried into effect. Just what that change would have meant, it is difficult to say because we had not the opportunity of discussing it. I should not be forecasting what the government intend to do at this session, but I have no doubt we shall have some substantial changes in the income tax. It seems to me the house is entitled to expect this inasmuch as we have had substantial increases in other lines of taxation. Having in mind the fact that the individual must of necessity have the income before he can be taxed, I cannot feel any great sym-

pathy for those who would oppose an increased tax upon incomes. I quite recognize the fact that there is double taxation so far as incomes are concerned, but is that not true in almost every other field of taxation upon which we are asked to make payments? Of course the municipalities and the provinces do not invade the field of taxation in regard to sales, but in many other respects we find duplication between the provinces and the municipalities. It seems to me, if an individual is in receipt, after all deductions are made, of a very substantial income, he should be called upon, particularly at times like this, to pay a much larger proportion of the taxation of the country than he is asked to pay under the present schedules. It is true I was a member of a government that reduced those schedules, but at the same time we were reducing commodity taxation as well. It is also true that hon. members to my left opposed those reductions, but we had a feeling that if we were reducing taxation, having in mind the fact that commodity taxation was fairly adjusted, we were entitled to make reductions in the income tax. Now that taxation is increasing, I wish merely to say that I am entirely in accord with the resolution that the government should take into consideration this field of taxation when undoubtedly they will have to make increases, if not all along the line, at least in a good many avenues from which they are now deriving taxes. For that reason, believing that the government are not precluded from taxing in other fields, I am going to support the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, just before you put the question I should like to make a remark or two upon this resolution. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has indicated that it was the opinion of some parliamentarians some time ago that income taxation should more properly fall within the jurisdiction of provincial government. I agree with that point of view. The Dominion government has the right, I presume, to place a tax on anything or on anybody, whereas the field of taxation for the provinces is very considerably limited.
I would point out that a motion to adjourn the debate is not debatable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Pardon me, Mr. Speaker.
I said that with the consent of the house I would withdraw my motion.

I was saying that the field
for provincial taxation is very considerably limited. As far as I am concerned, I agree

Federal Taxation-Mr. Irvine
with the point of view that this particular field should be left entirely to the provinces, but unfortunately the provinces do not seem to have awakened to the great opportunity which is here afforded them and they have not taken any action in that respect. I think such action should have been taken by the provinces long ago, and so for that reason the Dominion government might well perhaps set an example to them by indicating a field in which rich harvests might be reaped. At the present time the provincial governments are all in need of funds, as are all governments everywhere. I believe that there has been before the provincial government of Alberta a resolution somewhat similar to the one that is now under discussion here. I do not know, of course, what action the province of Alberta will take, but I do hope that they will impose an incpme tax. Meanwhile we have an income tax here, and the question is whether we should increase it or leave it as it is, in view of the present circumstances. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) took the ordinary course which finance ministers usually take in connection with a resolution of this kind when he pointed out that any action taken by this country in this respect must have a reasonable relation to the amount of income tax imposed in the United States in order that there might not be a flight of capital to that country. I do not think that the flight of capital argument need be very seriously considered at this time, for this reason:	Never perhaps in the history of
Canada was there so much money lying around waiting for an opportunity to be invested as now, and in face of that fact it is a strange thing that the provincial governments should be paying as high as six and in some cases six and a half per cent for the money that they borrow. If this is not ruled out of order, Mr. Speaker, I think that that practice is a very dangerous thing, for you cannot expect people to invest money in industry, where there is always a risk, when they can get six and one-half per cent from a provincial government guaranteed by the entire wealth of the province. I think that the provincial government should be raising money at three per cent, and if they cannot get it at that rate I think they should conscript it so as to force money into investment in other channels to give employment in this country. There is no danger of money fleeing from Canada to the United States at the present time because they have more money there than they know what to do with, just the same as we have here, and they have no place to invest it because no place is safe just now, and so there is no danger of
a flight of capital from this country to the United States.
I	ought to take the opportunity to point out that the Prime Minister perhaps misunderstood the point of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) when he drew a *contrast between one bill which asks for
311,000,000 and another which provides for the cutting of the salaries of the civil servants. The hon. member for Red Deer was not suggesting that there should be a repudiation of the debt, but rather that, without repudiating the obligation, there (Should be increased taxation upon those who stand to profit by 'the country fulfilling its obligations. That puts the matter in a very different light.
Another point which might be brought forward in connection with the criticism of the Minister of Finance is that there cannot be much danger of capital fleeing to the United States from 'Canada when in .this country we impose on a million dollar income a tax of $362,000, whereas in the United States the income tax on the same income is only $240,000. If capital will not flee when there is a difference of over $120,000 in income taxation on a million dollars, how much of a difference will it flee for, I would like to know? I would like to know just how far we can go safely and Still prevent it from fleeing. I would not mind risking going a little further and see what happens.
I think we all appreciate the point taken by the Minister of Finance, that he does not wish to commit the government in anticipation of the budget by stating to what extent the government will consider an increase in taxation in any respect, but I believe that he read the resolution somewhat narrowly, if I may 'be permitted to say so, for it merely asks that the government consider the question that any increase in taxation found necessary should take the form of adjustments in the Income Tax Act, in order that those best able to pay should be the first and most heavily affected. The point to be emphasized is that those who have the 'highest incomes should be the "first," and they should be asked to pay first because they have the money with which to pay. They also should be the most heavily taxed because they are the best able to pay it. I think the Finance minister suggested that if that part of the resolution had been a little more reasonably worded the government might have permitted it to go through without committing itself in anticipation of the budget, so therefore I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), that the motion
Federal Taxation*-Mr. Elliott

be amended by inserting after the word "that" in the fourth line of the last paragraph of the resolution the words "to the extent found possible."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How will it read then?
It would simply mean then, any increase of taxation contemplated would be imposed upon incomes to the extent found possible.
Should not the amending words be inserted after the word "increase" instead of after the word "that"?

Before the amendment is put, Mr. Speaker, I would like your ruling as to whether the original motion is in order. Personally I do not think it is in order for a private member to move a resolution involving the expenditure of public money.

The resolution simply asks that the government take the question into consideration. I think it is quite in order. Mr. Irvine moves that this resolution be amended by inserting after the word "that" in the fourth line of the last paragraph of the resolution the words "to the extent found possible."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That does not make sense.

I do not think the amendment improves the resolution at all. I can quite see the objections of the Minister of Finance. I am personally in sympathy with the spirit of the resolution, but the objection voiced by the Minister of Finance is I think that any increase in taxation found necessary should take the form of adjustments. That is absolutely mandatory upon the government. If my hon. friends would permit the resolution to be phrased somewhat along this line, that among the increases in taxation found necessary there shall be given consideration to adjustments in the income tax, it would I think overcome the objections of the minister and would also carry out the principle advocated by my hon. friends to my left.
Mr. SPEAIvMAN: I do not rise to address the house again, Mr. Speaker, but merely to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Would not the last paragraph read perfectly intelligibly in either case; that is, either in its present form, or with the words "to the extent found possible" instead of the words "found necessary"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I
indicated in the course of my remarks that

if this resolution had meant that the government in considering increased taxation should consider increased income tax, the resolution would be acceptable. But I do adhere to the objection which I took to the original motion, and which I think still obtains to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). In that respect I may say that I am wholly with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). If an amendment to this motion were couched in terms similar to those suggested by him it would be entirely acceptable to the government.
Amendment (Mr. Irvine) negatived.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) was good enough to let me have a glance at the comparative figures of income taxation in Canada and in the United States. There is attached a schedule of the new income tax that is likely to be imposed in the United States. I notice that our tax on a $4,000 is about three times as much as that levied in the United States- roughly about $16 to $5. But on an income of $100,000 the United States taxation is about double that of ours.
That in my opinion is the proper principle of income taxation. We are now in a very serious condition with regard to obtaining the money to carry on the administration of the country. We are at a point where taxes must be obtained from those who are best able to bear them. That, after all, is the real test of taxation. But whether this taxation is the most equitable or not, we have to resort to the means which will give us the required revenue. In other words, we must tax the people who are able to pay. I would suggest to the hon. minister that in his budget he follow the practice of our neighbours to the south to which he has just referred and make the higher incomes bear a much greater taxation in relation to the lower incomes than they do at the present time. I have no doubt from the manner in which my hon. friend referred to these comparisons that he has in mind to apply this principle when he makes his next revision of the income tax schedules. This should be done.

Mr. Speaker, after what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has said it is evident that the resolution will not pass in its present form. Being in sympathy with its principle, I should like to see it amended so that it might pos-

Federal Taxation-Mr. Gardiner
sibly pass in a manner acceptable to both sides of the house. Therefore would the minister consider the following amendment? To insert before the word "any" in the third last line the word "in"; in the second last line strike out the words "should take the form of" and insert the words "consideration should be given to." The last three lines would then read "that in any increase in taxation found necessary consideration should be given to adjustments in the Income Tax Act, in order that those best able to pay," and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can rise at this moment only with the consent of the house because I have already spoken. I did Dot follow my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I would need to have the text of his amendment before me in order to be able to express an opinion upon it.
I will read it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But it does seem to me that this debate will have served its purpose by expressing the opinion of those hon. members who have spoken. Obviously that is the chief purpose to be served. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) are very serious, for the resolution merely asks the government to take into consideration these things. speechtext: I do not want to quibble over language, though I must say it seems to me that the objection I took to the first amendment was sound. speechtext: I understood Mr. Speaker to say that it was the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, but the same objection holds good. I was dealing with the amendment itself and not with the source from which it came.

speechtext: While my hon. friend is on his feet will he elucidate, for the benefit of the house, the proposition as contained in the amendment, that the income tax payer is the man best able to pay? That is the first statement, and the second is that he shall be the most heavily affected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
