any rate, the point is that when you include the words "amongst increases" you very clearly remove the objection of the minister to the original motion, which might be interpreted by one who is a stickler for those things to indicate that no increases shall take place except in income taxation. Then the amendment says:	" Amongst increases in taxation
found necessary, adjustments should be made in the Income Tax Act in order that those best able to pay should be the first and most heavily affected." Is there any doubt in the mind of the hon. gentleman or of any other member of this house that those in this country best able to pay taxes are those who have incomes? So is it unfair to ask that they should have their incomes taxed heavily in the face of existing conditions?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) himself, defending the position of the government in connection with this resolution, quoted statistics to show the income tax paid in this country in 1931. He indicated at the same time that those who had incomes were contributing substantially to the pulblic revenue, * and had been doing so in past years. If he had read the statistics from another point of view he would have found out something else, namely that of some ten million people in Canada only 143,000, in round figures, have 
incomes upon which to pay a tax. If that does not demonstrate the concentration of wealth in a very few hands, a concentration which is at present increasing, I do not know how it could be demonstrated. Surely, therefore, in view of existing conditions a heavy income tax on those who have incomes is fully justified. But if the minister had taken the trouble to analyse the income tax figures further he would have found even more support for my argument concerning the concentration of wealth.
It is difficult to speak, Mr. Speaker, when the minister himself, the Prime Minister and everyone else across the way is occupied with something else. I suppose it does not matter much.

Go ahead; you are holding
up the business of parliament.
If my hon. friend is paying attention I am sure that is all that is necessary; his weight with the government will be sufficient to ensure proper consideration of anything he may recommend.
Very clever.

Yes, not
bad, considering that I had not much time to think it up. But I wonder if I may have the attention of the Minister of Finance for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
would postpone his vaudeville performance for a moment, as an act of courtesy, while I reply to a query put to me by an hon. member sitting close to my hon. friend.

I had no
idea I was putting on that sort of performance. I am debating in this House of Commons a matter of a great deal of importance at the present time. The minister is occupied with something else. I do not know what he is considering, but certainly his remarks are not courteous or in keeping.
When the Minister of Finance was making his analysis of the income tax figures, showing the enormous burden already carried by income tax payers he would have found an intense concentration of wealth in few hands in Canada. As I said, 143,000 people make enough on which to pay an income tax, but if my hon. friend had analysed the figures a little further he would have found that of the 143,000 income tax payers in 1931, some 6,600 paid about $21,700,000 out of a total of $26,100,000. In other words a little more than six thousand people paid almost the entire income tax received. The rest of income tax payers, 136,979, paid only $6,186,000. These

Federal Taxation-Mr. Campbell
figures can be traced back year after year and we find that the only difference is, not in the relationship between the two, but in degree as the income tax increased this incidence. In 1930, 6,014 income tax payers paid $20,959,000, while 136,000 paid only $6,500,000, in round figures.
The fact of the matter is that Canada, in common with the United States in particular -I separate these two countries from the rest of the world-has through special legislation, as the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) pointed out in her few remarks, and special bounties, bonuses and all sorts of grants of land and rights to power in thp past, laid the basis for great fortunes which to-day possess not only the wealth of this country but the great power that goes with it. We are in the hands of this government, and the government has an opportunity to serve the public and not wealth. The resolution introduced by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) urges upon the government to consider fairly in its budget proposals this year the taxation of wealth in order that the conditions of the working people in this country may not be further handicapped by the imposition of increases in duty taxation.
I doubt whether there is an hon. member who does not realize that in Canada in eight out of every ten households the family lives in the shadow of unemployment. Savings are not possible with the average wage paid in this country, if anything like a decent living standard is to be maintained. As a matter of fact, even in the civil service itself amongst the best paid wage earners in Canada, the average wage is only $1,500 a year, and that includes all the tops as well as all the very low salaries. It must be clear from such figures that the average worker, the average woman in Canada, has not an income upon which to maintain a decent standard of living and at the same time to save anything. The whole condition of this country typifies, in the present crisis we are faced with, a concentration of wealth under capitalism which in itself will destroy the capitalistic system my hon. friends are bo fond of, unless they take such reasonable steps as are now proposed to redistribute in the form of taxation the capital income and wealth of the nation. I have only this further to say. We have gone a long way to meet the views of the minister and I sincerely trust he will accept the amendment. If he does not accept it then I want to place myself on record as definitely in favour of the amendment and, if that is defeated, in favour of the original motion.

In
justice to the minister it is only fair to say that when he suffered some criticism at the hands of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) I was the one really guilty and not the minister. I had taken the liberty of consulting him for a moment to see whether it was possible to secure an amendment which would be acceptable to all sides of the house, and I therefore beg now to move a subamendment which I believe will cover the situation. In order to put the motion clearly before the house, as thus amended, I will read the resolution fully with the amendment I propose.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), that the resolution be amended by striking out all the words after "consideration," and adding the words, "a substantial increase in the income tax." The resolution before the house would then read:
Whereas, it is becoming increasingly apparent that the present methods and extent of federal taxation are inadequate to meet our requirements, and
Whereas, an extension of the principle of commodity taxation has been suggested as a means of meeting the situation, and
Whereas, the drastic fall in price levels and the consequent increase in the purchasing value of money has seriously affected the producer and business man, while being of corresponding benefit to those whose incomes, derived from certain classes of bonds, mortgages, etc, are still undiminished, if not increased.
Therefore, be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration a substantial increase in the income tax.

In view of the statement just made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), I sincerely trust the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) will accept my apology for what he considered was, although it was not intended to be, a vaudeville performance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before you put the subamendment, Mr. Speaker, may I say to my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) that I did take exception to his remarks and to the fact that he was apparently deriving some pleasure from bear-baiting me, as it were, in circumstances which must have been clear to him. I could not without an act of discourtesy to one who sits near to him direct my attention to the hon. gentleman, and I thought this must have been obvious to him, for usually he grasps a situation quite readily. In view of his remarks I am only too happy now to accept his statement and to assure him that he will find me at all times anxious to deal courteously not only with him but with every other hon. member of this house.
Federal Taxation-Mr. Rhodes

I- have always found the hon. gentleman most courteous in the past, but it was impossible for me to determine the character of the conversation or negotiations between the hon. member for Mackenzie and himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now that I am on my
feet I may say to my hon. friend that I must take exception to the attitude he assumed in his argument in discussing the question before the house. The hon. gentleman would leave the impression that in virtue of this resolution and the discussion this afternoon we are determining the question as to what shall be the income tax in Canada. That would be the impression he would leave; and a reading of his remarks on the hustings would clearly indicate that to be the case. Then he takes it upon himself to suggest that the government is resisting the idea of increasing the taxation of income. Furthermore, he attributed personal motives as well. He clearly left the impression that the Minister of Finance was a man of substantial income; ergo he would object at once to any increased taxation. Well, I may say that I am very much in the position of an individual down south. A wealthy northerner coming down the gangplank of a Mississippi river steamboat asked him whether he could change ten dollars, and he replied, "No, sir, I can't; but I thank you for the compliment just the same." My hon. friend from Bow River may be pleased to call me a wealthy person, but I assure him I must take his word for it. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend knows full well that there is a method as well as a time and a place for dealing with taxation, and it is not incumbent upon the Minister of Finance nor upon the government of the day when individuals, as they -have every right to do, bring forward a resolution dealing with taxation, thereupon to make a statement with respect to the subject. My hon. friend can be quite free in his arguments, but it is another matter entirely with one who holds a responsible post in government. As I say, there is a constitutional method of dealing with these matters.
Let me say that notwithstanding the sarcasm of certain of my hon. friend's remarks, to-day, we believe that any proposal having to do with taxation should be based upon the principle that those who best can pay should be called upon to pay the most. That is equitable taxation. I thought I made it quite clear in my original remarks upon the main motion that we were prepared to consider seriously an increased income tax, -but I took exception to the resolution because of the 
form in which it was drafted. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) was entirely acceptable to me and to the government. I do not raise the question whether or not this subamendment is in order; in any case if I did so the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) would no doubt say immediately I was actuated by some ulterior motive.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the sense that I have indicated, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) is entirely acceptable to me.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCO IS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to refer to the necessity of an amendment to the Bank Act to cover reports to be made by the different banks to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). We do not know how many people would be affected by a resolution similar to the one before the house. The banks now send monthly reports to the Department of Finance stating the amount of current and savings deposits on hand, but those reports do not give the amounts of the different deposits in each bank in each province. It might be agreeable to the minister to amend the Bank Act later on to provide that twice a year the banks shall report to the department indicating the amount of savings and current accounts for each province, and also the number of accounts under $500 and the number over $500. With this information we would know exactly how many people have substantial bank accounts. Because of the good will which has been shown in the house, I will not insist further upon this point.
Mr. Speaker, I have just one or two observations to make in regard to this resolution. I understand there is now before the house an amendment and a subamendment.

Do I understand the hon. members for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) to have withdrawn their amendments? The subamendment as now proposed is not an amendment to the amendment, it is an amendment to the main motion.

I have great pleasure in withdrawing my amendment in order that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) may move his amendment in the regular manner
Amendment (Mr. Gardiner) withdrawn.

Banking-Mr. Coote

I have no pleasure in withdrawing mine, but I will do so.
Amendment (Mr, Neill) withdrawn.
The question now is on the amendment of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell).

Mr. Speaker, I have just a word or two to say with regard to the amendment now before the house. I am in entire sympathy with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) with regard to the amendment which he has just dropped.
I understand that an announcement was made the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with reference to increased taxation along certain lines, but it must be understood that our support of this resolution is not to be taken as an indication that we will not vigorously protest against the necessity for increased taxation. We might find occasion to criticize very strenuously the necessity of such increases as might be made,in the income tax. I desire to make it clear at this stage that although we support the general principle of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie, we reserve to ourselves the fullest right of discussion in regard not only to the general principle of increased taxation but also to the particular proposals which may come down in connection with income or other taxation.
Amendment (Mr. Campbell) agreed to.
Motion (Mr. Lucas), as amended, agreed to.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the standing committee on banking and commerce be instructed to inquire into the question of banking, currency and credit in Canada, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing that they especially inquire into and report on the advisability of amending the Dominion Notes Act so as to eliminate the provision for redemption of dominion notes in gold and to provide for the issuing of dominion notes without relation to gold reserve.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, reduced to its
simplest terms this resolution asks for an investigation into the whole question of money, and I am sure the subject is of sufficient importance to justify the most thorough inquiry. Under our present economic system, money is the most important thing in life;
man must have money for his three primary requirements of food, shelter and clothing. Money means the chance to live. I think this fact is well illustrated by a story which appeared about a year ago in the Ottawa Citizen. A man had been held up on the streets of the city by a thug who pointed a revolver at his victim and said: "Hand over your money or I will blow out your brains!" The poor victim, without any hesitation, replied: "Go ahead and blow them out; I can live in Ottawa without brains but I cannot live here without money." I am sure the majority of hon. members will agree that his last statement at any rate is true and the same applies to any other part of Canada.
The amount of money which we control determines our standard of living, not only in the material sense but also in a social and intellectual way. Money is so important that the lives of ninety-five per cent of the people are vitally affected by what those in control of finance do to money or credit. If we are to have any chance of getting out of this depression this year, if we are to have an opportunity to get around that comer for which we are all looking, it will depend upon someone doing something to our money system. The providing of money for the carrying on of trade and commerce is one of the primary duties devolving upon the government of any sovereign state. Under our constitution this duty falls upon the federal parliament.
Parliament in its wisdom or unwisdom has passed the Currency Act which fixes the denomination and metal content of our coins. This act makes the dollar the standard unit of our currency and fixes the gold content of that dollar at 23.2 grains of pure gold. Parliament passed also the Dominion Notes Act, which provides for the issuing of paper money, known as dominion notes, against a certain gold reserve. It makes dominion notes legal tender in Canada except at offices of the Receiver General and provides for the redemption of those notes in gold upon presentation at offices of the Assistant Receivers General in Canada.
We have also the Finance Act under which dominion notes are issued to the chartered banks of Canada against the deposit of collateral security.
We have the Bank Act which authorizes the issuing of bank notes, that is paper money, to the extent of the paid-up capital of the banks, with certain excess issues in certain months of the year. It also provides that the banks may issue further notes against deposits in the
Banking-Mr. Coote

central gold reserves. The banks are also authorized under this law to make loans and to receive deposits.
Under this system authorized by Canadian law we had in this country under date of August 31, 1931-I am quoting approximate figures:
Gold held by the government.... $ 74 000,000 Gold and other coins held by banks 64,000,000 Gold held in central gold reserves. 13,000,000
Total	$151,000,000
That is the amount held in gold and subsidiary coins. We also had issued and in circulation in Canada at that date:
Dominion notes	 $141,000,000
Bank notes	 141,000,000
Then we had:
Bank deposits	$2,030,000,000
That makes a total, roughly speaking, of $2,300,000,000, all of which under our law would be redeemable in gold. May I point out that bank notes and bank deposits totalling over $2,100,000,000 are redeemable in legal tender, which would be dominion notes, and dominion notes outstanding at that time amounted to only $141,000,000. Dominion notes are redeemable in gold, but gold amounted to only seven per cent of the total money outstanding in Canada on that date, and in the term "money" I include only what we generally call cash, that is, coins and paper money and deposits in the banks.
Any unusual happening in the world may cause a demand among noteholders or holders of deposits in our banks for gold. If that demand is met and the gold paid out, the result is to deplete our gold reserve, and in that way restrict the issue of dominion notes. Dominion notes under our law are based upon gold and dominion notes are the basis for bank credit. Therefore, when the issue of dominion notes is restricted, it follows that the credit which can be extended in Canada is likewise restricted. The amount of credit outstanding in any country at any time is the main governing factor in determining price levels. When credit is restricted, prices fall; purchasing power is cut; business is curtailed; unemployment is created, and the whole vicious spiral of deflation is put under way. That is what has actually happened and that is the situation which we are facing in Canada to-day. Of course it first happened in some other countries of the world, but because of the gold standard Canada was compelled to follow the same policy as the countries which started this deflation.

I might point out here that to-day private citizens are being urged by bankers to pay their debts and the bankers are urging all governments in Canada to balance their budgets. They can do that only if they can get their hands on more money. The bankers do not seem to realize that under our present system the way in which the great bulk of our money gets into circulation is through the issue of bank loans. Wlien those loans are not issued, there is not sufficient money in circulation on which people can get their hands to pay their debts. If people cannot secure money to pay their debts and buy goods, governments are not going to be able to balance their budgets. In proof of the statement which I have just made, that it was the restriction of credit which caused the world depression, I should like to quote from one who, I think, might be regarded as an authority. I refer to Mr. R. S. Noble of the Royal Bank of Canada, who, speaking at last year's meeting of the Canadian Political Science Association, said:
In my judgment the main factor in bringing about and continuing the present world-wide depression has been the disastrous fall in the commodity price level and that this has been brought about not by over-production-
I am glad he said that.

tariffs, war debts, stock market collapse or any of the usual causes assigned but by a thoroughly stupid bank policy with France and the United States as the principal villains in the piece.
If a stupid bank policy was responsible for the world depression, we cannot get out of this world depression until we get an intelligent bank policy. May I point out again that because of our adherence to the gold standard, this thoroughly stupid bank policy which caused the world depression, caused the depression in Canada to be on a par with that in most of the other countries. Perhaps I might quote the opinion of Professor Gustav Cassel, one of Europe's outstanding economists, who said:
It can never be denied that the defects of the monetary policy of the United States are chiefly responsible for the present crisis in the world's economy.
What was this Stupid bank policy referred to by Mr. Noble? I have not time to go into the subject at any length, but I should like to point out again that under the gold standard, gold is the basis for credit, and on one dollar's worth of gold, from fifteen dollars to twenty dollars' worth of credit is created. The figures which I have quoted for Canada prove that.
The central banks of France and the United States, according to many authorities, have

Banking-Mr. Coote
hoarded between them nearly one-third of the world's monetary gold reserves. That amount of gold has been placed in their vaults; it has not been allowed to be used as the basis for the issue of currency, and consequently the world's credit has been restricted to the extent of many billions of dollars. When you restrict world credit to such an extent, you must upset prices and all the contractual obligations of the world which are expressed in terms of money. It is therefore no wonder that to-day the world is faced with the great problem of reparations and war debts. Debts which have become impossible of payment largely because of the manipulation of our monetary system.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is there any shortage of credit in Canada?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I really do not know how
to answer that question. I know that due to low price levels people are not able to get the credit they ordinarily could. The situation in the world to-day so far as gold and gold standard countries are concerned, might be likened to a game of marbles. Supposing a number of boys are playing marbles and two of them corner all the marbles. The rest of the boys have to quit playing or go and play some other game. To-day countries other than the United States and France should in their own interests play some other game than that of the gold standard. I may have said this before, but if so I want to repeat it: the amount of credit money in circulation largely determines the price of commodities and the world to-day is suffering from this depression because of the contraction of credit due to the hoarding of gold. I note that recently Mr. Hoover, President of the United States, is credited with saying:
Credit is the blood stream of our economic life. Restriction or destruction of credit cripples the revival and expansion of agriculture, industry, commerce and employment.
The paper 'from which this is quoted, the Ottawa Citizen, says;
To-day business is bad because of lack of purchasing power among consumers.
The great question facing Canada at this time is what can be done to restore that purchasing power. May I point out that the industrial system produces for profit, not for use, and a falling price level destroys the motive which makes the system function. The production of real wealth is curtailed because we cannot distribute the production among our people, and the reason we cannot distribute it is primarily because we have not enough money in circulation. I remember a year ago the statement was made that in
China millions of people were starving because China had no transportation system which would move food from the coast to the interior where the famine conditions existed. But we have not that excuse in Canada. , We have one of the finest transportation systems in the world and yet to-day some of our people, if they are not actually starving, are not getting enough to eat. We have the food and we have the railways to transport it; the only thing we lack is sufficient money in the hands of consumers.
I agree with what the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen said last year, speaking before the Canadian Bankers' Association at the Royal Y'ork Hotel in Toronto, and I am glad that he made this statement at that particular meeting. He said:
If people were in a position to exchange what they have too much of for what somebody else has too much of, we would see that there is not too much of anything. The trouble is that they are not in a position so to exchange. Were the facilities of exchange adequate, were the world's monetary system adequate to demands for exchange, then the three per cent increase in the world's products from year to year would mean a three per cent elevation in the standard of living each year for the masses of mankind.
I freely admit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a world situation. But we cannot permanently excuse ourselves by using that as an alibi. We are following practically the same policies as those other countries which we hold responsible for this depression, and how is the world ever going to get out of the depression if every country continues to do as we are doing-sitting with folded hands waiting for Providence to get us out? I suggest that we could take some definite action in Canada, and because I believe that our adherence to the gold standard has made the situation very much worse for Canada, one of the questions I should like the banking committee to inquire carefully into is whether we should any longer endeavour to adhere to the gold standard, and if so, why we should adhere to it. That is a subject that should be thoroughly investigated.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, When the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the question of the gold standard and stated that because of our adherence to that standard Canada was suffering unduly from the world
Banking-Mr. Coote

depression. In support of my statement I should just like to quote this passage from the monthly letter of the Royal bank for June, 1931:
It will be obvious that for countries operating on a gold basis the responsibility of the price level lies almost altogether with the central monetary authorities of the United States, Great Britain and France, which hold about 75 per cent of the monetary gold stocks of the world and influence the bulk of the liquid capital. At the present time, all other countries must conform to the composite policy of these three outstanding financial powers or temporarily abandon the gold standard, as has recently been done by Australia and two or three South American countries.
Since that was written Great Britain has been forced to abandon the gold standard. I think the same is true of Canada; that is, we have abandoned it so far as redemption of our notes in gold is concerned, although we have not yet taken legal steps to cancel our obligation to do so under the law.
Some people, of course, will ask: If the gold standard is to be abandoned what is to be the basis of our currency? Perhaps I could not do better than quote from an issue of Toronto Saturday Night of about the time Great Britain did abandon the gold standard. On that occasion this journal stated:
Ihe real basis of currency has always been the resources and the industry of the people in the countries which issued it. This is markedly true of Canada, which as Hon. E. A. Dunlop, provincial treasurer of Ontario, has aptly pointed out, has never been actually on a gold basis except for ipternatioual payments. Times like these demand realities, not myths, and consequently the suspension of the gold standard may be viewed as a hopeful event.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think the committee on banking and commerce might very well be empowered to inquire into the advantages and disadvantages of the gold standard. After all, the gold standard is simply a monetary policy. We should inquire whether it is the best policy for Canada, or whether it should be abandoned and a better policy adopted. I will admit that it has some advantages. It does lend us an air of respectability; and stable exchange rates are very beneficial for those having to meet commitments in the United States. But the disadvantages of the gold standard I am sure more than outweigh its advantages. It limits the amount of credit in Canada by the amount of gold in the treasury. It puts the price level in Canada at the mercy of foreign banks. Canada is a debtor country and if we are to remain on the gold standard we must be prepared to sacrifice internal stability of prices, wages, employment, and our whole standard of living. For what? For the sake of exchange rate stability.

Surely that is too great a price for us to pay. It is no use saying we cannot get a better system. I think a better system must be found or the whole capitalistic system is bound to collapse. It is to those who are interested in the preservation of the present system that I am appealing to-night.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will leave my hon. friend
to speak on that. At the moment I want to direct the attention of the house to the effect of our adherence to the gold standard on agriculture. The leader of the opposition in South Africa recently stated that the adherence by his country to the gold standard was crucifying agriculture. Our attempt to adhere to the gold standard, is, I think, crucifying agriculture in Canada. I am not able to devote very much time to this particular phase of the subject, but I do want to point out that at the present time the price of wheat, cattle and hogs in Canada is dependent upon the price which we receive for these commodities when exported. The bulk of our wheat is sold for pounds sterling. We translate the British pound, according to to-day's quotations, into $3.93 Canadian money. If our currency were at par with Britain's-and I think that is where it should be if it is to be at par with anything-the pound would represent $4.87 of our money. In other words, we are losing 94 cents on every pound sterling that we receive from the sale of our products in Great Britain. I should like again to remind the house that the prices we receive for the products we export-grain, cattle, hogs -set the prices of all those products when they are sold in Canada.
May I also point out that we are competing with the Argentine and Australia in most of these products? The farmer in the Argentine at the present time can translate the British pound sterling into the equivalent of $5.40 of our money; in Australia the farmer can translate the pound sterling into the equivalent of $5.80 of our money. I should like

Banking-Mr. Coote
to know how long the Canadian farmer is going to be able to compete with the farmers of the Argentine and Australia under those conditions? At the present time if our currency were at par with Britain's the price for the average steer sold in Canada would be increased by more than $10; the price of wheat would easily be increased by 15 cents a bushel. I have in my hand a page from the Commercial Intelligence Journal of September 26 last, containing a report from our trade commissioner in Australia. This as before Great Britain went off the gold standard. He says:
The exchange premium in Australia gives wheat growers an apparent gain of about 6i pence (13 cents) per bushel on all wheat exported.
That knocks our five cent bonus into a cocked hat.

The gold standard in Canada as part of our money policy is fixed first of all by the Currency Act which sets the number of grains of gold in our dollar, and further by the Dominion Notes Act. Subsection 3 of section 4 of the act provides for redemption of these notes in gold on presentation at any office established for that purpose. It is for that reason that I mention specifically in my resolution the Dominion Notes Act. I should like the committee on banking and commerce to be authorized to inquire into and report to this house as to the advisability of repealing or suspending the operation of subsection 3 of section 4 so that we should no longer be compelled to redeem our notes in gold. As a matter of fact the assistant receivers general in Canada are not to-day redeeming our notes in gold on demand. I have talked to different people who hhve endeavoured to get gold in exchange for notes and have been refused. The law still stands, and at the present time so far as I am aware-I speak subject to correction-we are evading the law in refusing to meet the requirement I have referred to. I should like the banking and commerce committee to be authorized to report on that particular matter-whether we should continue ostensibly to carry on under the gold standard and yet actually evade the act; or whether we would not be in a much better position if we simply repealed this subsection. Subsection 5 of the Dominion Notes Act fixes the gold reserve against which dominion notes shall be issued. I think in line with the report of the Macmillan committee there is no necessity for gold or other metallic reserve for our national currency, and that this section of the act might very well be repealed, so that the Finance minister might be in a position to use the gold to meet some of our foreign liabilities if he so desires.
I might point out to the house that the issue of dominion notes without gold reserve might be largely increased. If our issue of fiduciary notes were at the same ratio as recommended for England by the Macmillan committee, on our present gold reserve we could have issued dominion notes to the amount of $500,000,000 instead of $144,000,000 as at present. I think if this question were properly understood by the public generally the issue of a larger amount of dominion notes and their circulation in Canada would add to the stability of our system. I cannot see any reason why our gold should be tied up in a vault somewhere under the east block. I do not believe it is doing any good there to-day. I know there are certain people who refer to any money not based on gold as unsound money. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in his remarks last week, used the term "sound money" and by most people that phrase is understood to mean money based on gold. I should like to point out that if Canada had remained on the gold standard, or what is called sound money, in 1914 it would have lost us the war. We abandoned it then in a hurry, on half a day's notice, but we cannot abandon it now to cure unemployment.	To-day I think Canada is
engaged in a war against poverty, and it is just as important that we should abandon gold now as we did in 1914. If we are to stick to that kind of sound money I am afraid we may lose the war in which we are now engaged.
I think the words "sound money" are much misunderstood.	Right Hon. Reginald Mc-
Kenna, speaking at the annual meeting of the Midland bank a few days ago, had this to say with reference to sound money:
A sound unit of currency would always be of the same value measured in the aggregate of the things on which our money is spent.
That is what sound money ought to be, money with a stable measuring value. That is one of the principal purposes for which we use money. Mr. McKenna goes on to say that gold has never provided that, and then he states:
Viewed in that light, could any standard have failed more signally than has the gold standard.
Banking

Mr. Coote

He says he does not see any reason to doubt our being able to keep the purchasing power of money stable with what he terms a managed currency. I am sorry I have not the time to quote Mr. McKenna at greater length; to those interested I would recommend his speech, which appears in the Manchester Guardian of January 30. However, he does say:
The art of monetary management will have to l>e relied on more and more to obviate such catastrophes in economic life as we are witnessing to-day. We must not delude ourselves once again into thinking that if we return to gold all will be well. Renewed indulgence in that idea would be fatal.
I commend those words to the government and to every hjn. member of this house. Right along that same line, with regard to the question of managed currency I should like to quote Sir William Beveridge, director of the London School of Economics, who may be considered an authority on this subject. He said:
Liability to booms and slumps of production is bound up with capitalism, with making not for use but for profit, which depend on prices as prices depend on credit. Success or failure in controlling credit may thus prove to be the acid test of the capitalistic system.
I think Sir William's words are well worth the attention of the government and of the house.
I should like this committee to be authorized and instructed to inquire into this question: Can interest on the federal, provincial, municipal and railway bonded debts, totalling over five and a half billion dollars, together with corporation debts, real estate mortgages, bank loans and so on, be paid at existing price levels? If not, how can commodity prices be restored to the levels of 1925 or 1926? I should like the committee to inquire as to whether any action can be taken through the money system to make this payment possible. Let me quote from an article appearing in the Wall Street Journal under the signature of Thomas Woodlock, a regular contributor to that journal, on this very point of commodity prices. The article carries this heading:
Commodity Price Level Must Rise or Debts Will Be Sacrificed
I regret that I have not time to read the whole article, because I think it is splendid. The writer says:
It so happens that the world now finds itself with a volume of existing debt far beyond anything ever before existing in economic history, this because it gets its living by a system which basis upon credit-debt-as its very foundation. It is the pressure of this debt which is everywhere stirring an agitation for a change in the money units which measure the debts. What we are witnessing is an acute phase in the

process outlined by Mr. Feaveryear, and the heart of our present problem is to prevent this process from destroying the credit structure which furnishes the foundation of the world's economy. It is perfectly evident that the structure can be preserved only at the price of considerable sacrifice by the creditor class for it is surely historically true that loans which do not "produce" the means for this repayment are in the long run not repaid. Borrower may be slave to lender as the phrase goes but only in a limited sense; a truer phrase is that which says that blood can not be had from a stone.
On all sides are heard proposals for a change in the "gold standard" of the United States. Some are for plain issues of "non-interest bearing treasury notes" which, of course, are to be "unlimited legal tender for all purposes." Others are for	"bimetallism"-silver-and
others for some kind of "inflation" by means of large government bond issues with rediscount privileges for bills secured thereby. The instinctive revolt against the gold unit is widespread and is at bottom the direct result of the pressure of debt. One thing is becoming clear; that is that either the commodity price level must in the next few years rise to relieve the debtor or the creditor will have to write off a good part if not the whole of the debt. And, if commodities will not rise to the money unit, the money unit is quite likely to come down to the commodities. This is the fundamental significance of the departures which have already been made from the gold standard.
Coming from the Wall Street Journal, Mr. Speaker, I think a statement like that should not be ignored by members of this house. Then I should like to quote very briefly from a speech made by Right Hon. Winston Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer and the man who put England back on the gold standard in 1925. Speaking before the Economic Club of New York at the Hotel Astor, he said in part:
As to the solution of the economic crisis, Mr. Churchill said: "In my opinion, it would be sufficient at this stage if two or three of the principal governments of the world were to proclaim their intention of revaluatir.g commodities and services upon, let us say. the 1927 or 1928 level; and then if sufficient financial experts w'ere selected and told to devise steps by which this should be done, and the form of international currency that would be required to keep a stable standard of value hereafter, I do not think you would be setting them an impossible task. I expect they would find that there were several ways of accomplishing this purpose once it was clearly defined and authoritatively set forth.
"I would like to see the governments of United States and Great Britain, through their agents, the federal reserve and the Bank of England, come to the definite conclusion that commodities must be revaluated up to the 1927 or 1928 level, and that hereafter sufficient currency must be available to provide a stable measure of price."
Surely it is not difficult to deduce from that statement that Mr. Churchill believes the adoption of a proper monetary policy will

Banking-Mr. Coote
bring commodities back to the price levels of 1927 and 1928, and until the commodity price level is brought back to that point existing debts in Canada cannot be paid, with interest at current rates.
In the few minutes left to me I should like to point to what is happening in the United States. Recently at Washington two measures were adopted, the one providing for the creation of the reconstruction finance corporation, and the other the so-called Glass bill, widening the note issue privilege of the federal reserve banks. In regard to these measures the Financial Post contains an article headed:
U.S. Embarks on Inflation to Save Banks
I know there is a good deal of objection throughout the country to the use of the word "inflation" or to the process of inflation. It is more proper. to say anti-deflation or, as some writers now say, reflation. But call it what you like-inflation, anti-deflation or reflation-anyone who to-day refuses to use some such measures to put more credit in circulation and increase prices is as foolish as the man who refuses to put air in a flat tire for fear he may blow up the tire. Anyone who is driving a car with a flat tire will stop at the first service station and put in some air, even if it is not free. I remember hearing of a Scotchman who, the first time he saw the sign "free air" did use so much air that he blew out the tire. It is possible to blow up a monetary system with inflation, as was done in Germany years ago, but that is not what is proposed in the United States to-day nor is it what I am proposing in Canada. I simply advocate putting out sufficient credit in Canada to raise commodity price levels, and that is as sensible as putting air in a flat tire to keep up the proper pressure. The man who puts air into a tire uses a gauge and when he has just enough air he stops. Currency, I am quite satisfied, can be managed so as to put out, in Canada or in any other country where it is adopted, the proper amount required. I do not think there is any insuperable difficulty about that.
In my opinion there is more than sufficient reason for asking for this investigation. It seems to me that whatever other steps may be taken to lift us out of the present depression, monetary reform of some kind is absolutely essential. I should like to see the committee make a thorough and exhaustive inquiry into these matters such as was made by the Macmillan committee in England. If the committee did nothing but make a study of the Macmillan report they might suggest to
the house some measures that would be helpful. I had thought of asking that there be given to our banking committee a reference similar to the one given to the Macmillan committee in England, but I have been told that the committee in England found themselves limited by their reference. This is the reference which was made to that committee:
To inquire into banking, finance and credit, paying regard to the factors, both internal and international, which govern their operation, and to make recommendations calculated to enable these agencies to promote the development of trade and commerce and the employment of labour.
I consider that a splendid reference, but I should like to see the reference to our committee, if one is granted, made wide enough that they will not feel hampered in their investigation. If the committee considered they had not time to go as thoroughly into the question as they would like fco, they might suggest to the government the appointment of a commission along lines similar to the Macmillan committee. There are, however, two or three specific questions which I would suggest for consideration by the committee in addition to what has already been indicated.
First of all I would suggest this question: How can the purchasing power of the community be kept up to the point where we can consume the surpluses which our great industrial machine can turn out, so that we should not be faced, as we are at the present time, with poverty in the midst of plenty. I should like the committee to inquire carefully into the gold standard. As I suggested before, I should like an inquiry to be made particularly as to its effect on the basic industries of Canada-agriculture, mining, lumbering, fishing and other industries-and as to its effect also on employment. I believe that the return to the gold standard by Great Britain in 1925 did increase unemployment, and if that result followed in England would not a return to the gold standard increase unemployment here? I would finally suggest to the committee this question: If credit is the life blood of industry, why should the amount of credit existing in Canada depend on the amount of gold stored in the treasury vaults and which is never intended for circulation?
In short, I should like the committee to be asked to report to the house regarding changes Which might be made in the monetary system so as to enable us better to distribute among our people the goods which we in Canada are so well equipped to produce.

That was my impression of the remarks of the right hon. gentleman. Great Britain's trade policy had nothing whatever to do with her abandonment of the gold standard. Anyone who has studied the international byplay which has taken place in the financial world from 1927 to 1931 will know that a great European nation deliberately resorted to a carefully buttressed financial armament in order to obtain political domination of Europe. The boundaries of several states in Europe have been fixed by the financial policy of that great country. At the present time this country has two delegates attending the disarmament conference in Geneva and in the most friendly way I suggest to the administration that something more important is before the world to-day than the reducing of the number of ships of war, the reducing of standing armies and~t!ie reducing of the number of aeroplanes, submarines and the equipment and munitions of war; the greatest necessity of the world to-day is a comprehensive policy of international financial disarmament. I should like to see the Canadian delegates fighting to that end so that in the development of our national policies we shall not be compelled to suffer too much from these international factors which are at the present time directly affecting our Canadian national life.
A short time ago I had the temerity to stand in my place in this house and to advocate a qualified moratorium in Canada on

Banking-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
capital accounts. This afternoon the Prime Minister asked an hon. gentleman to my left if there was any shortage of credit to-day. To that question, my answer would be this: I think that every single individual to-day, at least within my experience, is suffering from a most distinct and emphatic shortage of credit. Every municipality throughout Canada and throughout the west in particular is being throttled by the restriction of credit. The four great provinces in western Canada have been so reduced to financial extremities that they have had to come to the Prime Minister and ask to be allowed to depend upon the weight and security of the Canadian treasury before they could undertake the ordinary processes of financing. I hope it is not true, and I hope it will never be true that this great Canadian nation will suffer from a restriction of credit.
I agree in the main with the observations of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I know that to-day business after business and industry after industry in my own province of British Columbia is being crushed out of existence because of the policies adopted by our Canadian bankers in refusing them any ordinary or generous extension of credit. When I say that I repeat what I said a year ago, that we should be proud of the record of our banks during the great crisis through which we are passing. However, I know industry is being forced out of existence and there should be some great liquidation of the frozen assets of our nation. As President Hoover has said, we must thaw out the frozen confidence of our nation. This has been partly accomplished in the United States by the creation of a $2,000,000,000 fund, known as the reconstruction finance corporation, of which my hon. friend does not approve. Apart from agreeing with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) in his contention that the high tariff barriers should be knocked down, I contend that one of the great necessities at the present time of the Canadian people is a real system of controlled inflation in regard to our currency and monetary system. The other day someone said something about a managed currency. In my opinion Canada has the best machinery in the world for a managed currency. Under the provisions of the Finance Act of 1914 and the act of 1923 there is vested in the Minister of Finance and his treasury officials sufficient power to enact to-morrow a policy of managed currency or controlled inflation without any alteration in the legislation except the repeal asked for by the hon. member for Macleod.
Let us consider what the Finance Act was responsible for during the great war. Let us 
consider what happened when in 1917 the Imperial government asked Sir Robert Borden for a loan of $50,000,000 to help them out in their struggle in those strenuous days. What happened? Overnight almost, a policy of controlled inflation under the system asked for was put into force and $50,000,000 were sent to England to help them over there. Canada did magnificent service at that time by suspending the redemption of dominion notes in gold.
Personally I agree we need in Canada more credit; we want to put an end to credit restriction; we want more confidence among the people; we want the banks, the money lenders in this country, to have less say in monetary and fiscal policies and have them laid down by the house and directed by the parliament of Canada through the government. The more we reduce the dual capacity of our Canadian banks, in the first place as money lenders and in the second place as dictators of Canadian financial policy, the better it will be for the Canadian people.
In conclusion I wish to say this: we have had in Canadian history several successions of great issues. In the first place we had provincial issues in the different provinces. Then we had the great battle for responsible government. Then we had the great debate entered into by the fathers of confederation. Then we had a fiscal policy which particularly since 1878 has divided the two main parties throughout the Dominion of Canada. Then unfortunately we had in our history some racial and religious issues which divided these two parties. Then we had a great issue that arose during the great conflict of 1914-18. But never in Canada have conditions of an economic depression forced a recognition of the necessity of all parties, regardless of previous principles or political affiliations, studying carefully the financial system and monetary method of our land. This is not a normal depression; this reminds me of some of the great European cataclysms of the past -for instance the fall of the Roman Empire, the renaissance in Europe, and the social, political and industrial upheavals in England and France in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Speaking for myself I say that the policy of the Liberal party at this time in Canada should be to look to the left, to look to the interests of the consuming masses of our people and not to be afraid to change any laws which are built up on class lines. The solution for the present depression will be found in fearlessly developing that policy which will be in the interest of the consuming masses throughout our Canadian land.

Mr. Speaker, because I have had the responsibility, particularly during the last few months and until a few weeks ago, of administering the Finance Act, I shall make, without further delay, the observations that I desire to make to this chamber.
I have followed with some interest the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), and his references to the technical side of the economics of the gold standard are worthy of a great occasion. But we are dealing with practical circumstances and facts. Unfortunately his knowledge of the issues of dominion notes is hardly accurate, as I shall presently point out. As for the suggestions made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), I think I shall be able to show to the chamber that if they were adopted it would mean the ruination of this country at this time.
In the first place, may I merely amplify very briefly some of the dbservations made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. Why is gold used as a standard at all? That seems to be the first question that might reasonably be asked. The answer is fairly clear. First, it is rare; second, it is convenient, and third, it has, by reason of those circumstances if you will, and others, a value that is uniform throughout the world. Hence it was, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, that it became the standard for values. It was worth just as much in Australia or Hongkong or London as it was in Paris or Washington or Ottawa. It had a fixed value that did not fluctuate with changing conditions. Therefore, for these and many other reasons to which on this occasion time will not permit me to refer, gold became a standard for values and we refer to it as the rare metal, the metal of value, and in other terms of that kind. We in this country, prior to and since confederation, have treated gold as a standard for values of our monetary system. I shall not do more than refer to the statute that is the law at the present time. That statute, with which I trust most hon. members are familiar, requires that the issue of dominion notes up to $50,000,000 shall be supported by a coverage of 25 per cent of gold. That is, when the Dominion of Canada emits $50,000,000 of its legal tender or promises to pay, on demand, there lies in yonder treasury $12,500,000 in gold, that being the ratio between the issue of paper and gold which we have by our statute provided. We have also provided that for any sum beyond $50,000,000 we shall have one dollar in gold for every dollar so issued. We also provide that ten per cent of all the deposits in the
Post Office Savings bank shall be covered by gold.
May I point out to the house that the hon. gentleman was slightly in error in connection with the present issue of dominion notes. If hon. members will turn to page 2188 of the Canada Gazette and look at the circulation and specie return for the 31st day of January, 1932, they will [DOT] find that we have altered slightly the form of the return as it used to be made in years gone by, believing it to be desirable that any person who wished to do so might by looking at that return ascertain exactly what the gold coverage of this country was with respect to our issued notes. First, under chapter four, 1915, there was an issue of $26,000,000. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat suggested that possibly $10,000,000 has been retired. I point out to him that the whole 826,000,000 is still outstanding. Then under the Finance Act of 1927, chapter seventy, there was an issue of $45,000,000. That represents the notes issued by the Dominion of Canada under the statute of 1915 and under the Finance Act, now being chapter seventy of the Revised Statutes of Canada for 1927, amounting to a total of $71,000,000. Then there has also been issued $99,382,805.69 in dominion notes, covered as to $50,000,000 by 25 per cent of gold and as to the balance dollar for dollar. Those three items-the $26,000,000 issued and still outstanding in its entirety, the $45,000,000 also issued and still outstanding in its entirety, and the issue of $99,382,805.69, make a total of $170,382,805.69. May I point out to the hon. member for Macleod that we still have outstanding at this hour over $71,000,000 of notes which are not covered by gold in any way, shape or form. So what he asks for has already been done to the extent of $71,000,000.
But further with respect to the $99,382,805.69 of dominion notes outstanding, it is only a matter of computation that it requires $61,882,805.69 worth of gold to cover them; that is, 25 per cent up to $50,000,000 plus dollar for dollar for the balance of $49,382,805.69, making a total of $61,882,805.69 which we have in our treasury to cover, may I point out to the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Mackenzie) not the $170,000,000 but only the $99,382,805.69 issue of dominion notes. That is provided for by the Dominion Notes Act. The result is that at the end of the month we had nearly $5,000,000 of gold beyond what was required. That is (a) ten per cent to take care of the post office savings bank deposits; (b) $61,882,805.69 to take care of the dominion notes outstanding under the provisions of the statute, by which 25 per cent.
