in connection with the fleet. You will all recall that immediately there came from Holland and the other continental countries vast sums of British securities. These were thrown upon the market on Friday afternoon and all Saturday morning for any price they would fetch. Securities wrere sold for fifty cents on the dollar, or even less than that. As soon as they were sold the seller demanded gold, and although the Bank of England stopped payment on Saturday noon-it was announced to the world on Sunday

the fact is that approximately ten million pounds in gold were taken from the bank Friday afternoon and Saturday morning. The result was the bank could no longer sustain the demand made for gold; the free market had disappeared; it could no longer meet the demands for gold in exchange for paper. That being so, late Saturday night the bank concluded to go off the gold basis and the Chancellor of the Exchequer made the announcement which appeared in the papers oa the succeeding day.
Now, look at what we had to do. It affords me an opportunity to tell this house, because the wisdom of what we did do has been questioned. The message to us was in cipher. It was decoded late Sunday night. It was impossible in the very nature of things to gather our colleagues about us. A decision had to be taken. What were we going to do? What would you say about your country under similar circumstances? Well, the statement I made, as you recall, was perhaps in fifteen words; I said it was for the people of Great Britain to determine what they would do but we would continue to meet our obligations in gold where we had promised to pay in gold. We had to do that or our credit was gone. We were deprived of the market for our securities. England being no longer in a position to meet any requests we might make for assistance, having failed to maintain her position as a free gold market despite the advances made by France and oy the United States in the form of gold credits, we were thrown upon one market and one market only-the market of New York. And not only that. Upon what we said that night depended the credit of this country. Let us have no misunderstanding about it. The international bankers of that city knew far better than some of the members of this house the terms of our Finance Act, our Currency Act, our Dominion Notes Act, our Bank Act. It is not necessary for me to do more than make that statement. They were aware therefore that technically since 1929 the country had been off the gold standard 
as the hon. gentleman has defined it, but we were still working under the provisions of the Currency Act which provided gold coverage in the terms enacted for our dominion note issue. I said we proposed to meet our obligations in the terms of our promises, and we have done so. The only reason we assisted the provinces was to enable them to meet their obligations in the terms of their promises; that is all. Of course it does not follow that this means there is any difficulty in the situation of the provinces; it does not mean that they have become bankrupt. It only means this, that for the purpose of meeting obligations for which they were not able to supply gold at the time, we had to assume the responsibility of helping them, and we have advanced money for that purpose. That is the position in connection with the application of the gold standard to our country.
The modern tendency is to believe that forty per cent is a sufficient average metallic coverage for bills. That is, instead of 25 per cent up to $50,000,000, and thereafter dollar for dollar, the modern thought is that if we have 40 per cent coverage for all our issues we will be safe. That is the generally accepted rule to-day, and you will observe that on the last day of January the total outstanding was $170,000,000. Forty per cent of that makes a total of $68,000,000, and you will observe that while we did not have that $68,000,000, nevertheless our coverage of gold so nearly approximated it that the credit of this country has steadily improved. I say frankly that but for Great Britain going off the gold standard, and but for the depreciation of the pound and the difficulties the pound has experienced, the dollar of this country would be worth par or practically par in New York. About that there need be practically no difficulty. That is the reason why this government has laboured day after day and week after week, first to create and then to maintain a favourable trade balance; because we could not face the possibility of having to pay in the only medium that would be accepted universally, gold, an adverse balance which a year ago, Mr. Speaker, was $103,000,000. We have converted that into a favourable balance where the gold due to us is between $10,000,000 and $15,000,000.
I do not ask you, sir, or this house to treat that as a great tribute to a government, because the Canadian people have done it. They have had to undergo many difficulties and many privations, and they have made many sacrifices to do so. It has inconvenienced many great merchants, but in the long

Banking-Mr. Bennett
run I am in the judgment of the house and of those who have given thought and consideration to the matter when I say that I believe if we had done aught other than we did we would have failed in our duty to this country at this time. I believe that will be the judgment of those who have given much consideration to the question. It may interest some of my hon. friends opposite, who should take an equal pride with us in the matter, to know that there are economists who say that the greatest single achievement that has been brought about by any country in the world since the depression has been that of ten million people in Canada, who have converted an adverse trade balance of $103,000,000 into a favourable balance.
Now we get down to the question of credit. I wonder if any man in this house will say there is a lack of credit facilities in this country at the moment, having regard to the security that is available for the credit asked. I have discussed the matter with men who have asked the banks to lend-what? It is not their money; for remember that the banks have no money of their own; their capital and reserves are locked up not only in buildings and facilities but in reserves of cash, and the money they loan belongs to the small and big people of this country who have their deposits in the banks. In nine cases out of ten my observation has been that when I have pinned down the applicant who complained, with this question, "Would you lend your money on that risk," in most cases, sir, he has said to me, "No." You go into the bank and ask for $1,000-of whose money? It is $1,000 of your neighbour's deposits, but you ask to borrow that $1,000 of your neighbour's deposits, and when the banker asks what security you can give, you say, "Well, I am going out on a farm. I have not got one yet, but I expect that I will be able to get a soldier settlement farm on reasonable terms; I am going to work it, and they will help me with respect to a crop." Do you think you would want your money lent on that security, if it was on deposit? Do you think that is a risk that would enable you to draw your money out of the bank when you write your cheque and present it? What is the reason that in the United States four thousand banks have failed in the last two years? It is because their assets were in securities that were not convertible into cash so that the cheques of their depositors could be met.
The business of banking is what? It is a simple thing; it is the maintenance of an equilibrium between demand deposits and demand loans and between time deposits and
time loans, so that you or I, drawing a cheque against that bank, may be certain that the bank will be able to pay what we call cash for it, notes, over the counter when the cheque is presented. In other words if my deposit has been put into a frozen credit that cannot be realized upon, the bank is insolvent, and that was what happened in the United States. That is the reason why this vast fund has been created in that country, at the instance of the president, for the purpose of enabling an organization to take up these securities that were not otherwise salable at the moment. When I say, sir, that the banking system of this country has been the sheet anchor of Canada in this period of depression,
I but state a commonplace. There is not one of us who, however small or large may be his deposit in a bank, cannot with certainty draw his cheque upon that fund to-day and know that it will be paid. The business of the Department of Finance has been to watch, to scrutinize and to care for the whole financial structure so that there should not at any one time be any such loaning of demand deposits upon time loans that when a cheque was drawn it could not be paid.
Now, sir, in the light of those facts is there a single member of this house who would say we should substitute, for a system that maintains a coverage of nearly 40 cents on the dollar for all our legal tender outstanding, a system under which there is no coverage at all? Where would your credit be? I put it to you, sir:	Where would your credit be?
That is the history of what has transpired. I could develop it further; I may have to do so before the session ends, but this affords a very reasonable opportunity to say to this house what I have said. The Bank Act will be up for revision next year, and there necessarily must be dealt with two or three large problems touching the whole banking structure of this country. One of them was alluded to both by the hon. member for Macleod and by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, namely a central bank. While our Finance Act enables the banks to come to the treasury and obtain legal tender, on depositing bonds of this country or of the provinces, or other prime securities, it will be observed that there is no coverage for these legal tenders thus emitted, and it follows that the question whether a central bank might not offer rediscount privileges and opportunities somewhat larger than those provided by the Bank Act is a matter well worthy of debate, especially in view of the fact that we have beside us the greatest credit organizations in the world. It might be possible to make a closer
Banking-Mr. Bennett

association with them by reason of the fact that you would substitute for a government organization a central bank organization which would not be the government itself but really an arm of government.
I want this house to understand that I am not expressing the view that a central bank is desirable. I am pointing out that the question is well worthy of consideration, that all has not been said about it that will be said, and all that can be said with respect to the question cannot be said upon the one side.
Under these circumstances, without labouring this matter unduly, for I have trespassed too long upon the time of the house already, I would say to my hon. friend from Maoleod that the Macmillan report was mot prepared in a day, nor was it prepared by any organization that might in any sense be compared with the committee on banking and commerce. I happened by accident to have a very brief discussion with the chairman of that committee while the report was still in preparation, and if you knew, sir, the amount of effort and toil and labour that was put into 'the preparation of that report, the number of people whose opinions were received, discussed and analyzed, you would realize 'how futile-I use the word not offensively-it would be to expect that from that committee would emerge a solution of this problem which we desire.
The opinions of individuals in their own country are of tremendous value. The opinion of a Canadian dealing with Canadian problems, knowing our nearness to the great republic to the south and our dependence, in a sense, for fresh capital, from the standpoint of the sale of securities, upon some country other than our own, when it gets beyond a certain limit.-all these are factors that must be considered and must influence the mind and judgment of the men who are to deal with them.
I therefore suggest to the house that the closest study be given by each individual member to all the problems that are connected with currency and credit, and with the allied and kindred matters that affect the financial structure of this dominion. If I thought for a single moment that to add, beyond $71,000,000 erf the present outstanding, unsecured ,paper money of this country, another twenty-five, or thirty or forty millions of dollars, would cure unemployment, would lift the depression and would end all our troubles, I would have no more hesitancy in asking the house for it than I have in asking the house to pass any estimate that is sub-
mitited to it. And there is not a member on either side of the house whio would hesitate for a single moment so to do. But in the end one has to give to these problems the best judgment one has, and at a moment such as this, when we have institutions that have stood the shock and stress and strain of the most difficult period in our history, financially and otherwise; when we have institutions that have thus sustained these shocks with credit alike to the Canadian, people and to the institutions themselves, difficult though it may be a-t times bo understand why we should not at once change these things, the answer is that there is no assurance in anything that has been said or any suggestion that has been offered, that to substitute the bald credit of the Canadian people for a credit that is sustained at the moment by $70,000,000 of gold coverage for the notes that have been emitted by the country is an experiment which this government dare not sanction. Moreover, if its credit abroad is to be considered, if our reputation for meeting our obligations is to be considered, does anyone for a moment suggest 'that we could substitute the notes of the Dominion of Canada-thousand dollar notes and others-to pay bills in New York? Does anyone suggest that?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: No one has suggested it that I have heard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The suggestion means
that or it means nothing. It can be of no value unless it means that, because there is $71,000,000 of inflated currency, using this language not properly nor technically, $71,000,000 of uncovered currency in this country at the moment, and we know the circumstances under which it was issued. For that reason and for many more reasons that might be given to the house, without going into a long and elaborate explanation of all the circumstances that have influenced the government with respect to each matter, we have been compelled to take decisions. And one of the decisions we have taken is that it is neither meet nor proper nor in the interests of this dominion that at this time this question should be thrown into the melting pot by a committee, not of experts, men trained for the purpose of considering them, but by a committee selected from the house of members, eminent in their own respective spheres, but, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has just said, untrained to deal with these problems. The proper time and place will be when the next revision of the Bank Act comes up, when opportunity will be afforded before a committee, select or otherwise as may be deter-

Banking-Mr. Pouliot
mined, to deal with the whole problem of the credit and financial structure of the dominion.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I do not wish to interrupt the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in his very interesting speech, but there are many anomalies in regard to the question of our currency and the gold reserve which I think should be explained. France, for instance, has a surplus of gold, and yet the franc has been stabilized at around 4 cents instead of 20 cents, which was the standard value. Again, England at the present time is receiving monthly about as much gold from India as is produced in the whole world during the same period, and at the same time the pound sterling is considerably below par.
There is one suggestion I would make to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). Reading over the report of the Department of Finance I was quite surprised to see that more than one-half of the assets of each bank in Canada is stagnant in immovable property. This explains the lack of circulation or the stagnation of credit. Will it be possible for the Minister of Finance to take that fact into consideration in order to facilitate the circulation of money by controlling to some extent the construction of bank buildings?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) had produced nothing further than the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and the speech we have just heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) it would have been well worth while. From different points of view, the presentation^ by each of these hon. gentlemen was certainly admirable, and their speeches will be instructive to those who are interested in the question.
The Prime Minister showed in his most able speech that he is better acquainted with theories than he would have us believe, and certainly he has all the practical knowledge which a man in his position could possess. Nevertheless, I wish frankly to take issue with the right hon. gentleman on some of the things he said. Though perhaps I have less practical knowledge than he has of the question under discussion, I represent another point of view, and inasmuch as there are several points of view possible I suggest that any view is certainly something which is well to the point and should be discussed.
The resolution which has been presented is similar to the one which passed the house in
1923, I believe. Unfortunately, however, the investigation that took place at that time was of no avail; the information which was collected by that committee was quietly buried, and all the expense involved in the study of the question was practically lost, except perhaps that the members of the committee had an opportunity to go exhaustively into the question. As has been stated by other speakers, this resolution asks that an inquiry be taken into the question of banking, currency and credit in Canada and also that the committee consider the advisability of amending the Dominion Notes Act to eliminate the provision for the redemption in gold of dominion notes.
The Prime Minister dealt extensively with the latter part of the resolution, namely, the danger to this country if we were to abandon the gold basis. The Prime Minister pointed out why gold was first selected as a basis for currency and credit. One of the reasons given was because it was rare. I must agree with that, but I answer that it is too rare. With all due respect to the difficulties with which I know the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) are faced, I contend that the thing is so rare as to be dangerous both to Canada and to all other countries.
The next reason given was that it was convenient. My reply to that is that it is not convenient enough most times, while it is too convenient on some occasions; it is too convenient at the present time for the well-being of Great Britain-it was removed just when she needed it most. The greatest difficulty with gold is that at the time we require it most, it is not there. It is too convenient in so far as its ability to be moved by others is concerned.	_
I disagree with the Prime Minister in his statement that gold is necessary as a standard. Gold never really has been a standard, nor do I expect it ever will be. Let us look at the absurdity of it. According to the statutory provisions referred to by the Prime Minister, for the first $50,000,000 of notes issued by the dominion we must have twenty-five per cent in gold; for all above that we must have dollar for dollar in gold. Let us apply that principle to other standards. Let us take the standard by which we measure energy, the unit of horsepower. Let us suppose parliament passes an act this year whereby we must develop no more horse-power from our water resources or our coal than we can provide living horses. Would anyone say that that was an intelligent thing to do? Yet we are asked to have a unit of value, we are told that we can have only as many units of value in circulation as
Banking-Mr. Irvine

we have gold dollars hidden away in some vault. I would not mind that if we had the same power to create gold as we have to raise horses, but we have not. The amount of gold we may have depends upon many factors beyond our control, and this makes it almost absurd to speak about the thing at all. As a standard of value it has never been adequate, and the requirements in respect to its being a standard are positively absurd. We do not require a horse for every horse-power of energy developed in the country, and we should not be required to have a gold dollar for every unit of value issued by the state to carry on its ordinary business.
The Prime Minister pointed out that there are $71,000,000 of notes outstanding to-day against which there is no gold. We know that those $71,000,000 of notes are as well backed as any note backed with gold. Canada does not have to limit her backing to one commodity; all commodities required by mankind have a value and behind that $71,000,000 is not only the wealth of Canada and what they may produce but also the good faith of the Canadian people, which is even of greater importance.
I understand the Prime Minister to point out-he will correct me if I am wrong-that we have coming due in the United States approximately one million dollars per day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Outside of Canada.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is an unfortunate fact
that we have borrowed too much outside of Canada. Of course, that cannot be charged to this government or to any particular government, but we must deal with the facts. What do we get from the United States or any country when we borrow money? Do they give us gold? No. Do they give us their bank notes or their state notes? No, they do not. When we borrow from any country we get merely a line of credit, which we had before we went to borrow. There is no reason why any undertaking, industrial, private or public, could not be financed by credit issued in Canada direct without having to go to New T ork or other parts of the world for it. The unfortunate plight in which Canada finds herself to-day has been caused by her borrowing so much, in terms of gold, from other nations. With the present restriction on gold she now finds herself called upon to meet those obligations in gold. This is a situation which we should seek to remedy; we should borrow at least within the British Empire, or, preferably from ourselves.
The Prime Minister stated that if the section of the act dealing with the redemption in 
gold of dominion notes were repealed our dollar would drop to possibly twenty-five cents. I submit that the Prime Minister did not sufficiently amplify that statement. As he has said, we already have outstanding $71,000,000 of notes for which there is no gold backing, and the dollar has not dropped to twenty-five cents. Why then could we not issue some more without seriously reducing the purchasing power of the dollar? I suggest that if such issue were not sufficient to inflate the currency, values would not be affected at all. And what is inflation? There can be no inflation in any country as long as there is not more money in circulation than there are goods upon the market to be purchased by it. No one will say that there is not a good deal of room in Canada for more money to be circulating than is circulating at the present moment. Why not issue the proper amount, and not so much that all value is lost?
Strangely enough, the further we go off the gold basis the more gold will be secured. How did France get all the gold she has? She got it by stabilizing her franc off the gold basis and thus created abroad a tremendous demand for her own goods. Her export trade became so great that she did not require to take goods in exchange and demanded gold, the result being that she pulled the world's gold into her vaults. The same thing would apply to Canada. If we were a little further off the gold standard than we are at present our export trade to the United States would be greatly stimulated. We could take payment in gold for the resulting favourable trade balance and before long we would have more gold in this country than we can hope to have by maintaining the gold standard.
I do not intend to follow this matter any further in its technical possibilities than is absolutely necessary to indicate ithe points in the Prime Minister's speech with which I disagree. I come now to the next point raised by the Prime Minister in respect to that portion of the re-solution which refers to credit. He asked: Is there a lack -of -credit facilities in Canada? I reply, most -certainly not. Our credit facilities are admirable, -perhaps equal to if not better than those to be found in any other country. The next question propounded by the Prime Minister was: Is -there any lack of credit security? Again I answer.
I do not -think there is. He then asked: Is there any lack of credit being issued? He answered this question himself in the negative. He held, as I -believe all bankers will hold with him, that for every well-secured proposition for credit put up to the banks they are ready to give credit. I believe that is -true,

Banking-Mr. Irvine
but these are not the questions we want to ask in connection with the proposed inquiry. Let me state the question which I believe we must ask and which is more important in connection with the matter immediately before the house .than the ones which the Prime Minister propounded. It is this: Were price levels lowered in Canada as a result of credit contraction, or was credit contracted as a result of the lowering of price levels? That is the question which has to be settled. At the present time price levels are so low that the returns on many investments will be very doubtful, and perhaps no amount of security would be considered adequate to cover a loan under present conditions. If a man is engaged in the manufacture of boots, where the price level is so low and business so poor, no matter how good his factory may be, he may have difficulty in securing credit. The same applies to agriculture; the same applies to any industry in Canada. Supposing any hon. member to-day had $1,000,000 that he wanted to place: where would he invest it? Would he invest it in railways? Not in their present condition. Would he invest it in agriculture, either in this or in any other country. No. Would he invest it in .coal mining? No. Where would he find a place to invest that $1,000,000 in the hope of having a reasonable return upon his investment?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: In government bonds.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, government bonds
would be the only thing left in this country or in the United States in which it would be considered safe at this time to make an investment of that sort. The question we want to ask is: How did that situation arise? Did price levels drop so as to discourage investment and to impair credits in that regard because credits were first contracted by the banks, or is the reverse the case? That is a question that is surely worth while investigating. I do not think it would be difficult to discover the truth of the matter were we to go about it as investigators. I imagine that the really accurate figures of price levels in Canada month by month over the past few years would indicate to us where the price level began to drop sharply, and the banking records would indicate very clearly when credits began to be contracted. If by a comparison of the two, it should turn out that banking credits began to be contracted before prices began to fall, we would be right in assuming that the present depression came about largely through the action of the banks in the first instance. That is the question to be settled, and I do not see how it can be
settled except through such an investigation as has been suggested by the hon. member for Macleod.
I think the investigation is very necessary also because of its educational value not only to the house but to the country No one will deny that the question of finance is more in the public mind to-day than it has ever been before in our history, and no one will deny that there are few subjects upon which there is more abysmal ignorance generally than there is on that question. So, if for no other reason than that we might bring a more accurate knowledge of the subject within the range of the general public, it might be well worth while to have an investigation of this sort. Further, I think we ought to have an investigation because of the fact that next year the Bank Act will be brought up for its decennial revision. It is too late to start to think about that when we are busy revising the act; the time to get the information which should guide us in the revision of the act is now, a year ahead. I recall the last revision of that act. We came here to tackle the revision of a very long and complicated piece of legal machinery. A large proportion of the members of the banking committee are at all times neither lawyers nor bankers, and if they are to do justice to their position they have to wade their way through every part of that statute and try to understand it. If as a parliament we are going to do justice to that act, we must get information beforehand. The proposed inquiry would be of assistance in preparing parliament for its task of revising the bank act next year.
I think there is a great deal of force in the statement of both the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and of the Prime Minister that the banking committee is perhaps not the best kind of committee to investigate a subject of this nature. The banking committee for one thing is too large and cumbersome and the time at its disposal will be much too short to make the investigation that will be necessary. But just because it is true that the banking committee is not the most fitting body to investigate finance, that is no reason why we should drop the investigation entirely. Therefore, in spite of the more or less definite attitude of the Prime Minister, I hope he will reconsider the possibility of having an investigation. The question is not whether we want to go off the gold basis; the question as I see it is this: have credits in Canada, by adherence to the gold standard or basis, been so limited in volume as to have done violence to business and industry? Another question which deals directly with credit is this: Were
Banking-Mr. Irvine

credits contracted in Canada iby the banks prior to the drop in the price level, or did the price level drop for some other reasons, with the result that the banks contracted their credit? The settlement of that question would be of great advantage in forming a policy. How can that knowledge be obtained without adequate inquiry?
In conclusion, may I suggest that with a greater knowledge than we now have of the subject, and if there is a definite relation between the volume of credit issued at any given time and the price level, it might be possible in future so to draft our Bank Act as to maintain hereafter some control of the volume of credit, thereby controlling price levels and also preventing a recurrence of a period of depression such as we are passing through at the moment. Therefore with all these considerations I submit that we would be well advised to cariy on the investigation proposed. If the banking committee is not the best equipped body to do so, let us find another committee, a special one or even a commission. The only objection I have to a commission is that commissions of that sort are composed, usually of bankers, and they always find that we have the best banking system in the world; that the gold basis is inevitable and that no other policy need be considered. That is the unfortunate thing about commissions on financial matters. Such results as I have stated have been the history of commissions in other countries, and I fear we would obtain similar results here if we were to follow a similar course. But even at 'he risk of that, I would be more in favour sf having a royal commission investigate this natter than of having nobody investigate it. May we not hope that the government will consider amending the resolution, if they so desire, so that it may go to some committee which will be competent to investigate a question of such importance to the people of Canada.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is a great privilege to be able to take part in a debate of such importance, one on which so many very able speeches have been made. The field has been covered pretty fully. There are, however, a few points that I might touch upon which might be fresh.
First of all I will deal with the first part of the resolution which asks for an investigation into the question of banking, currency and credit. The second part has already been fairly well covered by other hon. members.
'Mr. Irvine.]
I am in favour of this investigation for the simple reason that when in 1923 an investigation was obtained, just before the Bank Act was revised, the excuse made when we asked for certain changes in the Bank Act was that there was not time then to go into the matter. But if an investigation were made this year we would be able to study the information obtained and thus be in a better position to make changes in the Bank Act a year hence. Nine years ago the then president of the Canadian Bankers' Association made the extraordinary statement that nearly all the changes that had been suggested and eventually incorporated in the Bank Act had been put forward by the bankers themselves. When one appreciates that the Bank Act is, or at all events should be, a bulwark to stand in support of the rights of the people against the private banking institutions, it is indeed surprising that such a statement could be made. But it was simply because the public generally left this subject severely alone, with the result that those most directly concerned with the Bank Act, the bankers themselves, took good care to change the act as they saw fit.
It may be just as well to briefly review how a bank is brought into operation. It is still a question whether it is wise for those who are applying for a bank charter to be compelled to subscribe $500,000 capital, of which $250,000 must be paid up. Is that sum too large or not large enough? The question might also be raised with regard to the privilege that is given to banks when they get their charter, to issue an amount of currency equal to their paid up capital. That is a free issue; it is doubling their capital practically at the cost of printing. The question might also be raised with regard to the five per cent of their paid up capital which is retained by the Finance department for the note circulation redemption fund, and on which three per cent is allowed by the government of Canada. One might also very well ask for further information with regard to this fund.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that the banks are permitted to issue currency for one-half of the'ir paid up capital?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
To an amount equal to
their paid up capital.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who holds the securities?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is no security. It is a privilege that is given to the banks when they get their charter. They are allowed to issue in currency an amount equal to their paid up capital.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And give no security?

Banking-Mr. Spencer

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
agency through which they could use their credit. Every savings bank deposit we took in we had to reloan, and we therefore made less profit on it, because we lost the interest we paid to the depositor. That is how the business is carried on, and that is why in good times or in times of war when we have to extend the medium of exchange, a great deal of new money goes into circulation.
As to inflation and deflation, these subjects have been handled so well by other speakers tfeat I will not attempt to go over the same ground.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What money did you lend
in those cases?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Money is a credit created by collateral and drawable by cheque. If the hon. member would give this subject the consideration it deserves, which I am sure some day he will

and I am confident he will make a very good student when he does-he will know that money is like a concertina, it can be extended or contracted at will by those who control credit. Banking to-day is largely a bookkeeping system, and the sooner we realize that the better it will be for everybody.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the collateral you took became frozen, as has happened in the United States, how would you manage?

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is where the skill of the banker comes in; he should not take any frozen securities. I want to point out that although the Dominion Notes Act allows us to issue notes up to $50,000,000 with only 25 per cent backing in gold, above which amount we are supposed to hold a dollar in gold for every paper dollar issued, the act might just as well be repealed, for under the Finance Act we can and do issue dominion notes to an unlimited amount to the various banks that bring securities to the treasury board to be discounted. These dominion notes are also payable in gold, but there is no gold behind them. Therefore if we issued under the Dominion Notes Act fifty million dollars worth of notes with 25 per cent gold behind them and under the Finance Act another fifty million dollars worth of dominion notes to the banks against the securities they brought to the treasury board,, we would have one hundred million dollars of dominion notes out with only 12J per cent gold' backing. It will be seen that the Finance Act at once undoes what was intended to ibe guarded against by the Dominion Notes Act. Not that I am critical of the Finance Act; I think it is one of the best acts ever put on the statute book.
IMr. Spencer.]
If we had an investigation as suggested by this resolution the committee might go into the question of interlocking directorates. For instance, it may not be generally known that Sir Herbert Holt of the Royal Bank is a director of upwards of one hundred and thirty-five corporations. Is it likely that a director of various corporations in different lines of business, who has a great deal to say with regard to the functions of a particular bank, is going to encourage the starting up of another business competitive with his own? Again it might be asked, is it in the interests of western Canada that the headquarters of all the chartered banks should be either in Toronto or Montreal?
The Prime Minister's statement with regard to the payment of gold interested me. He said: We made a promise that we would pay in gold and we have kept that promise. That might have been done in New York, but it certainly has not been done in Canada. Not that I am worrying about it, because I take the stand that it is not necessary to have gold behind dominion notes for internal circulation. Thekte Mr. J. G. Saunders, Deputy Minister of Finance, wrote me a letter with regard to the gold basis, in which he said:
The gold basis, so far as Canada is concerned, would require-
First; that the banks should redeem their note issues in gold when required;
I hardly agree with him there, except that I would say that the notes of the chartered banks are payable in dominion notes, and dominion notes in turn are payable in gold.
Second; that gold could be exported and imported at will; and
Third; that Dominion notes would be convertible into gold when required at the various offices of the assistant receivers general.
To-day none of these things can be done and therefore, accepting those views, we are not on the gold basis. I should like to place on record one or two statements made by Mr. McKenna, chairman of the Midland bank, in his report to the shareholders of that bank the other day. He said:
The time has gone by for the childlike belief that as long as a country is on a gold standard all is well.
Again he said:
The world crisis is due in part to the inefficient working of our monetary machinery.
Referring to England going back on the gold standard in 1925, of which hon. members will remember he was very critical, he said:
For upwards of six years our monetary authorities fought a losing battle on ill-chosen ground.

Finally I will quote:
"Monetary policy has a powerful and a direct influence on the prosperity of each one of us, and if it is misdirected no one escapes.
Because I believe in the statements made by this eminent banker, and because I am entirely in sympathy with the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Macleod and the other hon. members who followed him on this side, I am in favour of the resolution now before the house, from which I hope it will receive sympathetic consideration.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the financial policy of this and all outstanding countries of the world is not of recent growth; it is something that has grown up and developed over a long period of years, and it is too much to expect that it will be changed in a short time. However, a great deal of attention, time and study is being devoted to the subject to-day, and I should like to see every member of the house take the advice given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and study this question, take it up seriously and try to secure all possible information upon the subject before the revision of the Bank Act next year.
Until very recently the men who questioned the orthodox system were generally looked upon as theorists, faddists or radicals with no practical experience, who were developing certain theories of their own. However, within the last two years particularly many outstanding and powerful bankers, big business men and statesmen, men whose word and authority cannot be questioned, have been asking serious questions about the banking system, inquiring whether or not that system might be modified to better serve the needs of the human family. Therefore I propose, Mr. Speaker, in the quotations I am going to place on Hansard tonight, to confine myself to the orthodox class rather than to university professors or students, or others who might be looked upon as theorists.
The question as to what is behind our dollar bill, the paper dollar, has figured very prominently in this debate, and on several occasions it has been pointed out that the ability to deliver gold, or something like that, is after all the only thing that makes the dollar bill worth anything. Let me say that the ability to deliver goods or something of value is the only thing that creates any value or any confidence in the dollar bill. It is not necessary that gold be delivered. Any citizen of Canada, securing a piece of paper, a dollar bill or a ten dollar bill, will set its value at what he can secure for that bill at the store or some other place. If he can secure certain 41761-42
Banking-Mr. Campbell
goods or services for it he is not going to inquire very deeply into the question of whether or not be can get gold. The main thing is the ability to deliver goods or services which is behind the issue of that piece of paper.
The question then arises as to what is the gold standard. Many refer to it as something that is fixed and determined, something that cannot vary from one day to the other. As a matter of fact it is as variable as the seasons. The gold standard is an ever-shifting, ever-changing thing. Some years ago the gold standard was whatever the Bank of England determined it should be. England was the great banker of the world, and what she said the gold standard should be was the gold standard. To-day the position has shifted and the United States has become the banker of the world; whatever the United States says constitutes the gold standard is the gold standard to-day. Not more than twenty-four or thirty months ago the gold standard of the United States meant that behind every paper dollar in circulation there was 38 cents or 40 cents in gold. To-day it means that there is 80 cents behind every paper dollar, so the gold standard has changed to that extent. It is as though a man contracted to deliver a certain amount of wheat, we will say, on the basis of four pecks to the bushel, but when he delivered the wheat he found that the standard had been changed to eight pecks to the bushel, and he was compelled to deliver twice the quantity for which he contracted originally.
I quite appreciate the position of the Prime Minister and the government in respect to a departure from the gold standard. The fact that we have tremendous obligations maturing regularly in the United States has imposed a terrible hardship not only on the federal government but on our provincial and municipal governments as well, because of the fact that we have to pay a great deal more than the value of our Canadian dollar. That is one of the difficulties with which we are faced today, but as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) pointed out, there is a moral in that situation, and perhaps in future we should try to do less borrowing in the United States and more at home. When we turn over a bond to a Canadian citizen we simply agree to repay in the currency of Canada whatever that may be, whether or not it is on the gold basis, so maturing bonds held in Canada do not impose on us any such obligation as is imposed by bonds maturing in the United States.
Recently the United States embarked on another policy, which I think in time will

Banking-Mr. Campbell

bring the gold basis back to the old standard so that there will not be more than 40 cents or 45 cents, or perhaps only 35 cents, behind each paper dollar. That is a policy of tremendous inflation, and I predict that before very long our dollar will be back at par in New York, not because we have done anything, not because there is any more gold behind our dollar, but because the United States dollar will have been devaluated and because more paper money will have been issued against the amount of gold in store.
In dealing with this question some time ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) pointed out very clearly how utterly impossible it was for the "debtor nations to pay their obligations to the United States in gold. He pointed out that the whole world production of gold,- if it were in the hands of those nations and used entirely to pay off debts to the United States, would not be sufficient to meet those obligations. I wish to quote now from an article that appeared in the Wall Street Journal, written by Mr. Thomas F. Woodlock. It is reproduced in the Financial Times of Montreal. One could hardly find two more orthodox sources than the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times of Montreal, and yet this article seriously questions the efficacy of the gold standard and of the present banking system, and asks some grave questions as to modifications in that system. The writer points out first that in connection with the gold standard there are three main rules that should be adhered to. In the first place he says that gold should function primarily as a central bank reserve, and its only other function should be its occasional use in settling international balances. Secondly, and this is very important, he says that the creditor country should follow a liberal tariff policy. It seems to me that the great depression through which the world is passing to-day is due to the fact that the United States, when she became the great banker of the world, the great creditor nation, did not follow the traditional policy that a creditor nation should adopt. For generations, as long as England was the great banker of the world, she was prepared to accept her dividends, her annual payment, in goods, and so long as she did that trade flowed naturally through the channels of the world. When, however, the United States became the great banker she either was not prepared to do this or she did not understand the rules of the game and therefore raised tremendous tariff barriers against her debtors. She said, in effect, to those countries that owed her money, "We will not take

goods." As a consequence these countries shipped all the gold they could get until today there is an impasse; and until the United States changes her policy in this regard she certainly will be in no position to collect debts. That is pointed out clearly in the Wall Street Journal. This writer quotes an author by the name of "Peregrinus," who was writing in the London Times. He points out, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us some time ago, that the whole world production of gold outside the United States is not sufficient to meet the obligations, and that something must be done. He pointed out that if France and the United States, the two creditor countries, continued to observe the policy already described, then in his opinion there was only one course for the debtor nations to follow and that was to depart from the gold standard and get along as best they could without it. He then deals with the question of managed currency, one that has come up quite frequently in debates in this house but with which at the moment I have no time to deal. This writer points out that it is quite possible and feasible for those countries that are forced to go off the gold standard to arrange a managed currency in order to maintain a stable price level in their own domain, and they could then ship their reserves of gold to the United States and France in settlement of debts so far as they could. He also states, and this is important, that the moment these other nations went off the gold basis and the United States and France were left on the gold basis, the gold itself would immediately drop in value; its only value then would be for the purpose of filling teeth and making jewellery. It might therefore be an easy matter ultimately for these countries to settle their debts. He goes on to say that after all, the way things are going at the present time, these reparations and debts will not be paid at all. that the depression will continue until that fact is recognized and admitted all round, and that the spirit in which the admission is made will be of great consequence to the peace of the world during the next few years.
The question of a managed currency-and that is the only alternative to the gold standard-is one that was dealt with a few years ago by Maynard; Keynes, recognized as one of the outstanding authorities of the world. As I understand the theory of managed currency, it is that those who have the responsibility of managing it should take a certain index price. Say there are one hundred different commodities-wheat, copper, coffee, butter, hogs and so forth-and that the index

Banking-Mr. Campbell
price is established at 175. Now, the men managing that would have to watch the index carefully. At the end of a certain period if they found that the price 'had dropped, that is that commodity prices had gone down, they would realize that one of two things had happened; either that the volume of business had increased, in which event there would not be sufficient money properly to handle the situation, or that the circulating medium, the amount in circulation, had decreased and' was forcing prices down. In that case they would be faced with the responsibility of putting more money in circulation. On the other hand, if -prices had advanced, their duty would be to restrict money. The banks would be forced to call in loans and that would have a stabilizing effect, forcing prices back to their proper level. That is the theory of managed currency put forward by this writer and at the present time it is being endorsed by outstanding bankers as well as by men prominent in political and industrial life.
May I again refer to the article in the Financial Times of October 3, 1930. The very heading of -this article is significant:
Bankers favour abandonment of gold standard.
This appears in the Financial Times of Montreal. I have not the -time to quote from this as extensively as I should like to, but I will deal with it briefly. The statement is -made:
The downward trend of commodity prices has reached the stage where the efficacy of the gold standard is being seriously questioned by economists.
Further on it says:
It seems reasonable to assume that if central banks throughout the world insist upon maintaining their present standards of gold reserves, the phenomena of declining price levels over a considerable period of time may be observed.
And again:
The corrective for the monetary situation of sharply falling commodity prices is an easy money policy. An intelligent control of the value of gold is regarded as essential to improve economic conditions.
It goes on to point out the direct relationship between the amount of money in circulation and the commodity price levels. It shows clearly that if the amount of money is restricted prices will drop, and if the amount of money is increased prices will rise. The great problem we are facing in this house, the subject which is most discussed throughout the country, is unemployment. Now for thousands of years, for countless ages, one of the great aims and objects of the human race has been to have more leisure for study and medi-41761-m
tation, more time to enjoy oneself; and that very urge in the human heart has brought about the development of the machine. The machine in turn has displaced labour, giving mankind the very thing that has been asked for throughout the ages. It has given the human race more leisure. And that really is what unemployment is. I hold that the term unemployment is a misnomer; there should be no such word in our vocabulary as unemployment. Perhaps I cannot boil down into one word the idea it conveys, but I should call it an improper distribution of goods and services. People are not unemployed because of scarcity, for, as many have pointed out, this is an age of plenty. Never before in the history of the race was there as much food and clothing, as much in the way of service, transportation, electrical power and so on, for the good of the human race. Yet in the midst of all this plenty there is poverty. What we require more than anything else is a stabilization of prices, and it is borne out by many distinguished bankers that this is dependent almost entirely on the amount of money in circulation.
I come back to the Financial Times, of October 16, 1931. Prominently displaj^ed on the front page is an article by H. S. Denny, a consulting engineer of Toronto. I quote:
The granaries of the world are bursting with corn, and warehouses are choked with goods, yet hungry hordes are steadily increasing in numbers. They stand waiting in despair until the capitalistic Lords of Creation, under the guise of a benevolent solicitude, find some profitable method of bringing the producer and consumer together again.
The familiar picture of children flattening their faces against the plate glass of a candy shop display, mouths watering and suffering from an almost intolerable desire, is, in some respect, a small scale illustration of the world condition to-day. A few pennies-helter-skelter into the shop, money paid over, candies received, jaws vigorously working, happy children and consummation of trade.
Then rather significantly the writer says "but they have to have the pennies." The article continues:
The bankers of the grim poker game called "life" have decreed that chips shall be excbang-able only for the commodity called "gold," and with scrupulous care and unscrupulous methods, have taken infinite pains to corral all but an insignificant percentage of that metal in their own vaults. There is no escape from the game. All human beings must play-there is no choice -be the stakes large or small, and willy-nilly the player must provide himself with chips or starve.
I direct the attention of the house to the fact that this article does not appear in a radical paper; it appeared in the Financial Times of Montreal.
Banking-Mr. Campbell

In connection with over-production, of which we hear so much to-day, I should like to refer the house to a pamphlet which has been published by Sir Henry Strakosch, G.B.E., a distinguished financier and economist of Great Britain. He lays down the general principle that there never has been over production, it is under consumption. After giving some figures of his own he bolsters up his argument by quoting Mr. Carl Snyder, the statistician of the federal reserve bank of New York. Again I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that this is not from a radical source, it is from an extremely orthodox source. Sir Henry points out that Mr. Snyder contends that during the past fifty years production has been increasing in the United States at the rate of about four per cent per annum compounded annually, while world production during the same period increased at the rate of three per cent, the world population increasing only by one per cent. That is, the production of the world on a per capita basis has doubled in fifty years. He goes on to point out that in the same period the consumptive ability of the human race has doubled. We are using radios and motor cars, we are wearing more clothes, eating better food and living in more comfortable houses than we were many years ago. Mr. Snyder has pointed out that this is capable of infinite expansion. Sir Henry asserts that the amount of money in circulation determines whether goods shall be consumed or shall pile up in the warehouses to create this thing we call overproduction. To quote directly from his pamphlet, he says:
A symmetrical increase of production of this kind in effect raises the standard of life of the people, and that, it is almost unnecessary to say, is capable of practically infinite expansion. No disturbance in the exchange of the greater output of commodities need, or does, arise in these circumstances, provided there are available media of exchange in the form of money of all kinds to an amount that corresponds to the increased volume of exchanges that this greater production necessitates. If it is available the general level of commodity prices will remain stable. It is only when the available amount of money is either less or more than is needed to effect these exchanges that the general level of commodity prices will fall or rise as the case may be.
I again quote from another extremely orthodox source, the representative of the great Mussolini. A despatch from Paris dated November 26 in connection with the opening of the disarmament conference, quotes Senator Boriello of Italy, as follows:
It is insufficient to disarm the military forces of the world. We must disarm the international bankers. We must have tariff disarmament fust as we have reduction of weapons.

It is my conviction that there will never be a permanent improvement in conditions until the outstanding nations of the world agree on some monetary policy, whether or not there is gold behind it, to provide elasticity sufficient to meet the growing needs and changing conditions. Of course, Canada cannot control world conditions but she can do her share to set her house in order, she can reorganize her monetary system to an extent to prevent any sudden drastic upsetting of the commodity level; she can provide sufficient safeguard to prevent the sudden and violent deflations of currency which have occurred during the past few years. I refer again to the Financial Times, the issue of January 16, 1931. The article from which I intend to quote refers to the now famous speech of Mr. C. E. Neill, vice-president of the Royal bank, and to the remarks of Sir Herbert Holt made on the same occasion. These remarks startled the whole banking fraternity because they questioned the orthodox system. The editorial reads:
A bank president who speaks with the voice of assets totalling nearly nine hundred millions of dollars (after a year of deflation) is entitled to speak with authority.
The article states that a remarkable change has been taking place in the opinion of leading bankers as to the necessity of a rigid adherence to the gold standard. In referring directly to Mr. Neill's remarks, the editorial says:
But he made it very clear that the standard could only be adhered to if a much greater degree of wisdom were shown in the international management of the gold supply than has been in evidence since 1918. Perhaps the most significant sentences in his whole speech were those in which he stated that if the principal central banks of the world had decided, upon the collapse of the stock market boom, that drastic contraction of currency and credit were not to be permitted, they could have effectually prevented the fall in the price level; after which he went on to say that "the countries with fiat currencies, such as Argentina, Uruguay and Spain, are not suffering anything like as acutely as the gold countries."
I have many other quotations which I would like to make from the Financial Times, but I see that the clock is moving rapidly towards eleven o'clock and I will have to cut them short.
I should like to refer briefly to an article which appeared in the Financial Times of September 26, 1930. This article comes from New York and in dealing with the gold standard it refers to the figures of Sir Henry Strakosch, already quoted. It refers also to Sir Josiah Stamp, a gentleman not unknown in

Banking-Mr. McIntosh
Canada. Sir Josiah is quoted as asserting that the menace arising from the inefficient use of gold "is the worst danger that eight years ago any of us could have feared, and finding us drifting still further into economic disaster." The article continues:
Sir Josiah Stamp appears to agree with Sir Henry in scouting the convention that the severe decline in commodity price levels in the last fifteen months is due to overproduction brought about by rationalization and mechanization. Sir Henry argues that since the rise in the volume of production had been in progress for the last half century while the level of prices had risen steadily up to the war, there should have been no price break in 1929, provided the available money increased in proportion to production.
Again may I quote from another editorial in the Financial Times of October 24, 1930. In part, it says:
A few days ago the Manchester Board of Trade addressed an extended argument in the nature of a petition to Premier MacDonald of Great Britain, calling attention to the fact that our volume of world business was increasing and our gold supply decreasing, and arguing that this would result in a fall of prices and an ever-increasing depression. The report of the gold delegation of the League of Rations recently was to the same effect. It stated plainly that the world was facing a "gold shortage."
In conclusion I wish just to refer to a very interesting article in Saturday Night of February 6, 1932. This is by Doctor Donald M. Marvin, economist of the Royal Bank of Canada. I have not time to put on record the quotations that I should like to give, but I suggest that ihon. members who wish to acquaint themselves with the intricacies of this question, should read this article, coming as it does from a representative of one of our outstanding Canadian banks. This man disposes of the bogey of over-production. He refers to the Malthusian theory of population, that is that the human race must Starve or be killed off because we cannot produce food rapidly enough to take care of the increasing population. He says that to-day the problem has developed from the opposite angle. He goes on:
As far as present day society is concerned, neither the picture of severe deficit nor of unlimited surplus is descriptive. . . . Basically speaking, there is no general overproduction within the confines of civilized society.
He goes on to point out that it will be necessary before long for those countries hoarding gold to turn it to use, that is to issue more paper against it or else the gold itself will become of nlo value. This is exactly what is happening in the United States to-day. The United States has found that the sterilization of the gold there may mean that the gold itself will ultimately lose its value, and to-day they are issuing huge amounts of credit against it. Doctor Marvin further points out that present conditions forcing, as they are, other nations off the gold standard, are going to compel these nations to work out a managed currency. I have not time to elaborate the point, but this is the economist of the Royal Bank of Canada laying down quite clearly the idea that a managed currency without gold is not only possible but very probable in the near future.
I would say again that I hope all members in the house will take the Prime Minister's advice and devote some time and attention to the study of this all-important question before a revision of the Bank Act comes up again next year.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH: (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, I did not intend until this afternoon to speak on this question, but during the last few days we have had quite a discussion on the currency, banking and credit problem, and as a member from Saskatchewan and western Canada I thought I had better say a few words on the matter. I listened with a great deal of attention this evening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) discussing this very important problem of Canadian banking and credit and I am free to say that I think he made one of the best speeches that I have listened to in the house so far as he is concerned.

Because I did not intend for a minute to say it signalized a clean sweep, but I want to be fair about the matter, and after abstracting from it any politics that hon. gentlemen opposite might have thought entered therein, make a candid admission that he gave a really fine exposition of the subject under review this evening. I do not think it does any harm to make an admission of that kind in the house in a matter of such moment. From the standpoint of quantity there was not too much to it, and from the standpoint of quality and volubility it was a fair sample of what one might expect from the opposite side of the house. There should be a good deal of credit coming to the Prime Minister for standing on the financial bridge of the ship of state and directing Canada during the last few months in such a way that the credit of the provinces has been taken care of and the credit of the dominion by his firm stand maintained in the markets of the world.
But I am free to say that I disagree with the Prime Minister when he intimates, as I think
Banking-Mr. McIntosh

the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) also did in the house last week, a doubt- mark you, Mr. Speaker-that on both sides of the house that we had that ability, that financial training, that would make it safe for a banking and commerce committee appointed from the 245 members of this national commons to investigate the question of banking, credit and currency of Canada. I am afraid I must disagree with any member who takes that stand. I am one of those who believe that not always does every member stand up and discuss a question when it comes before the commons, whether he is well posted on it or not. One cannot tell by the number of members who discuss a question as to the developed ability of the house on it. That is a certainty.

speechtext: The hon. member is making the Prime Minister's speech.

maintopic: BANKING, CURRENCY AND CREDIT ISSUE AND REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES WITHOUT RELATION TO GOLD RESERVE- PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, I am not. I am making my own speech. I believe we have in the house dozens of members who, on the spur of the moment and without any preparation by going through scrapbooks, newspaper clippings and files of the last five or six years, can make an intelligent speech on the question of banking and finance. That is my conviction.
I want to go a little further. I believe if that be the case-and I do not think it can be disputed-when the revision of the Bank Act comes up next year, we ought to have one of the strongest possible committees appointed from this chamber and, if it is necessary to nationalize that committee, let us do so. But let us get busy and make a thorough preparation for that investigation into the banking, currency and credit of Canada which must be made next year before we can say whether this or that part of the Bank Act must or must not be amended. We want to be sure of our ground, and for this purpose we must begin to make preparations now. I do not know what is in the Prime Minister's mind; I do not know whether or not he intends to leave this revision of the Bank Act until the next session without in the meantime making any preparation by way of the appointment of a national committee which might ultimately cooperate with a special committee of the house. If h.e does, then I am a little doubtful as to the report of that committee. But if so the committee should be appointed early in the session and given instructions as to what to do, I believe the ability that could be secured on that committee would measure up well to its responsibilities and a report would be turned in of which the House of Commons and Canada would not need to be ashamed. It is a question largely of time, not ability.	'

Further, may I say I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) trace the history of money in a word, telling us how society has revolved around the dollar bill or the various kinds of money preceding it throughout the centuries and how as a result we have been brought out of the realm of savagery and barbarism into the definite stages of civilization through which we have been passing during the last few centuries. That is an interesting evolution and I listened with rapt attention to the hon. gentleman while he unfolded the tale. He gave an excellent analysis of the question. Then I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) who, as one of the members of the official opposition, analysed the banking, credit and currency problem very carefully and successfully, and indeed, put the matter before the people of Canada so squarely as to state in definite and clear language where the Liberal party stands in respect to it, not only on the prairies and British Columbia but right across the whole dominion.
I think the Prime Minister made a very important point when he said that every member of this house should give this matter individual attention during the next year. I believe that every member has been giving it a fair amount of study, but when we consider what we have to do next year in revising the Bank Act, I think every member should give the question more attention than ever. As one of our great scientists has said, I believe there is no question which the human mind can ask to which it cannot in time give an answer. Every question, therefore, that we can ask about this problem we can surely answer if we will but patiently analyze the facts and dig up the answer. By getting a satisfactory answer in regard to this intricate question the development of society, the adjustment of agriculture and industry, and the building up of Canada as a whole will follow more naturally as fitting results.
Although the question of banking and currency and credit is undoubtedly a big one, one of the great questions before Canada and the empire and the whole world, I am not going to admit that it is the biggest question. I do not believe that it is. I believe that international debts and reparations are big problems, and that disarmament is another big problem. These are two of the big problems before the world, international debts and reparations, and disarmament. After those two I would place equally in importance, or even beyond them, the tearing down of extreme tariffs right around the world. These problems, three in

Banking-Mr. Coote
number, are equally as big as, if not bigger, than the question of banking and currency. They all go together, and we have to fight them in a block, and by fighting them in a block we can gradually overcome each one of them, and thereby strengthen the financial fabric of Canada and the empire of which we form a conspicuous part.
In conclusion, may I say that apart from the discussions that have taken place in the house, the big objective before us is what are we going to do at the Imperial conference?
I am very glad that this problem is to come before the conference, but I do not think that that is all that we ought to do about it.
I believe that the question should not only come before the conference, but be exhaustively analyzed there and the people of Canada be given the facts. We want the people educated along the line of this resolution. But beyond the analysis at the Imperial conference, and beyond the investigation we must have in this house in 1933, when the Bank Act is revised, there is no question that there should be individual preparation on the part of hon. members, so that everyone will know where he stands on it, thus doing his part to educate the people of his constituency so that we shall be able to bring united pressure to bear on this problem and the questions connected with it-international debts and reparations, disarmament and high tariffs-so that in the very near future these problems will have to fall down before the intelligence, the courage and the ability of those who are out to make Canada a bigger and better dominion and a more conspicuous self-governing unit in the British commonwealth of nations.

speechtext:
It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that in the short time at my disposal I cannot refer to all the statements and points of interest which have been brought out in this debate. I would, however, like to refer to the suggestion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that somebody had inferred that if we only got away from the gold standard it would bring in the millennium in Canada. May I say very emphatically that I do not believe that anyone ever suggested such a thing, but undoubtedly there are a lot of people in Canada who do expect the Prime Minister to bring in the millennium, and I am quite sure that so long as we remain on the gold standard he will not be able to do so.
I would also like to refer to the statement made by the Prime Minister that there was no shortage of credit facilities in Canada. I think I am stating the case fairly when I say that there is no credit in Canada for agriculture, Canada's greatest industry, and I do not see how that industry is going to continue to function unless credit for it is forthcoming. There is certainly credit for governments in Canada, but at what a cost? Recently two of our provinces floated loans to secure moneys for which they are paying six and a half per cent interest. If the interest on these loans is to be paid, it must be paid out of production. As Sir Thomas White, Canada's war-time finance minister said, speaking of Canada's victory loans:	If
the interest was ever to be paid it would be from the top six inches of Canada's soil. With the present prices for agricultural products, lumber products and mining products, how is the interest on these loans at six and a half per cent ever going to be paid? It is absolutely impossible. We are heading for a port which we shall not be able to reach so far as the paying of six and a half per cent on these loans is concerned.
The Prime Minister, either very carefully or accidentally, avoided one of the points raised in the resolution before the house. It asks the banking committee to inquire into the advisability of amending the Dominion Notes Act with a view to eliminating the provision for the redemption of dominion notes in gold. The Prime Minister dwelt at great length upon the fact that we should meet our foreign obligations in gold; that is, bonds maturing in foreign countries. No one to-night, so far as I know, has challenged that position. But under the Dominion Notes Act, Mr. Speaker, the dominion notes are redeemable in gold. Subsection three of section four of the Dominion Notes Act provides:
Dominion notes shall be redeemable in gold on presentation at branch offices established, or at banks with which arrangements are made for the redemption thereof as hereinafter provided.
